FIVE plus a per-opcode set for :583: deepseek. FOUR (pairing): glm, minimax. **The two pairing seats both cite #337's shared `warned_badlen` as the licence -- and that precedent is measurably not a licence.** agy and grok independently derived that #337's two sites are the two arms of ONE ENDIANNESS BRANCH (:709 `if (cpu->byte_order == EMUL_LITTLE_ENDIAN)`, :739 its `} else {`), so they are mutually exclusive at runtime and sharing loses nothing. grok put it exactly: *"two endian copies of one check, not a licence to pair different events."* kimi added an independent refutation from THIS ROUND'S OWN WITNESS: the :160 over-read fired with NO DISK ATTACHED, so no overrun could have occurred -- **the two ring halves are causally independent, which is precisely what the pairing assumes they are not.** DESIGN SETTLED: six per-instance flags, wrap ONLY the `fatal()`, leave every guest-visible side effect outside the guard. *** Q3: FOUR SEATS INDEPENDENTLY LOCATE THE REAL DEFECT AT :145, NOT :160 -- see `wdcringambig`, filed. *** glm: *":145 is an emulator error, do NOT latch without fixing the ring overrun."* minimax: *":145 IS a real defect that the latch does not fix -- it corrupts the ring and continues, so a TODO is owed there."* kimi located it first and most precisely. grok: *":145 is the unfixed pckbc/asc wrap, not a twin of the measured :160 flood."* Only agy said :160 was the site to worry about, and it was answering the question as the brief framed it. *** Q5 WAS CONFUSED IN THE BRIEF AND THREE SEATS SAID SO. *** grok: *"Q5's per-opcode (d) mutant contradicts the per-instance design the brief actually proposes -- that mutant is a spec change, not a floor test."* minimax and agy said the same. deepseek dissents usefully in the other direction: :583's diagnostic VALUE is the opcode, so a single flag hides distinct guest actions and a 256-bit set would preserve it. **Disposition: per-instance scalar for the fix (it is what stops a guest cycling 0x00..0xff for 256 lines); deepseek's per-opcode proposal is a SPEC IMPROVEMENT and is filed, not folded in.** The real (d) mutants, from three seats: scope `d->error |= WDCE_ABRT` INSIDE the latch at :583 (agy -- the second unknown command then silently SUCCEEDS); nest the `return (uint64_t) -1;` inside the guard at :160 (agy -- corrupts inbuf_tail); and **reuse a GUEST-RESETTABLE field such as `d->seccnt` as the latch (glm)** -- the sharpest of the three, because the guard then reads a field the guest controls. *** THE :145 WITNESS IS NOT A ONE-STORE WITNESS, AND codex SUPPLIED THE TWO HONEST ROUTES: *** prime `head = WDC_INBUF_SIZE - 1, tail = 0` in the detector and call the producer once; or, for a real guest-path measurement, attach an image and issue **513 undrained IDENTIFY commands** -- each adds 512 bytes through `wdc_addtoinbuf`, and the final byte of the 513th reaches the 262,656-byte wrap. The second route needs `landiskdisk`. *** AND A DETECTOR RULE FROM codex THAT APPLIES TO EVERY ROW: each site row must FIRE THE SITE TWICE. "A one-off first warning proves announcement, not suppression." *** A row that triggers a site once cannot distinguish a working latch from no latch at all -- which is this project's vacuity floor, stated for the latch class specifically.  *** A WRONG RECORD IN THIS ROW, WRITTEN BY ME AND CAUGHT BY THE ADJUDICATOR. CORRECTED 2026-08-25. *** Earlier in this note minimax is attributed the position that :145 is a real defect the latch does not fix, and is COUNTED AMONG SEATS SAYING DO-NOT-LATCH. **That count is FALSE.** minimax's Q3 says verbatim: **"So: latch both."** Its position is latch-and-mark, which is the disposition this round adopted -- it was recorded as dissenting from a ruling it agreed with. *** THE DON'T-LATCH CAMP IS glm ALONE *** ("`:145` is an emulator error, do NOT latch without fixing the ring overrun"), which turns a 2-of-8 reading into 1-of-8. **AND glm's OWN FALLBACK SILENCES HARDER THAN THE LATCH IT OBJECTS TO:** it proposes "downgrade it to `debug()`", and `debug()` has the early-out at `core/debugmsg.c:375` -- free-running at `verbose == 0` gives `v < 0`, so it vanishes ENTIRELY in production, while a latched `fatal()` still announces the first occurrence and cannot be silenced by `-q`. The dissent's remedy is strictly worse for the property the dissent defends. **Weigh deepseek's Q5 dissent knowing its ring analysis was the panel's weakest:** its ":145 is a guest error -- the guest wrote more data than the ring can hold" is factually off. The EMULATOR writes that ring on the guest's behalf; the defect is state representation. *Second time in two days that a seat-count in this project's records was wrong in the direction flattering the writer's own ruling. The tally was never the argument -- but a misquoted seat is a wrong record whichever way it points.*  *** ADJUDICATED 2026-08-25 (fable5, main-loop hat, on 8 of 9 mandated seats -- PROVISIONAL on its face w.r.t. the absent ninth, per that seat's own rule). *** **(1) Q5 UPHELD, two sharpenings.** Scalar per-device flag at :583 this round; deepseek's per-opcode set FILED. Per-opcode-versus-per-device is a SPEC choice, and deepseek's framing ("the scalar IS the (d) mutant") is circular -- it assumes per-opcode is the baseline and then calls the alternative a weakening. Clause (d) tests the CHOSEN spec's repair; it does not adjudicate between two acceptable specs. Put per-device in the CONTRACT (clause e) -- "does not claim per-opcode uniqueness at :583" -- so a later alternating-opcode observation is OUTSIDE the contract rather than a floor breach. **SHARPENING 1, the best single point of the panel: the two-different-opcodes row SHIPS ANYWAY, with the expectation INVERTED -- ONE LINE TOTAL.** Same stimulus deepseek wanted, opposite oracle. It kills a last-warned-opcode implementation (under which an alternating 0x5a/0xaa guest floods forever) AND pins the per-device spec in one row. **SHARPENING 2: the filed item inherits a TWO-membered framing and must not.** Honest weakening of my own precedent: #337's latched messages at :816 and :855 carry NO VALUE PAYLOAD -- :583 is the only site whose message names an opcode -- so "three latches in this file" is weaker precedent for discarding value-resolution than it looks. The filed option set is THREE-membered: scalar (shipped), per-opcode set (deepseek), and the in-tree COUNT-BOUND idiom (`n_trunc_msgs`, `src/cpus/memory_rw.c:495-523`) -- which this row already banners and which nobody in the dispute named. **(2) `wdcringambig` DOES NOT BLOCK.** The latch bounds the announcement to first occurrence; it does not silence it. **The corrupting store is ALREADY SILENT TODAY** -- :141-146 stores, advances, then tests, so the wrap line fires once per 262,656-byte lap and the N+1th store that destroys data prints nothing. What the latch removes is repetition of a late, miscorrelated warning. THREE OBLIGATIONS make it honest, all in-round and cheap: (a) /* #NNN */ comments at :145 and :160 naming `wdcringambig` -- "latch bounds the announcement; the ring invariant is untouched"; (b) the detector CONTRACT disclaims ring health, and the :145 primed-state row is marked for re-pin under the oracle-correction rule when `wdcringambig` lands; (c) file glm's dissent VERBATIM into `wdcringambig` as provenance. **THE TEMPTING THIRD PATH WAS CHECKED AND REJECTED FOR A MEASURED REASON.** grok and kimi both prefer restructuring :145 to the pckbc #288 shape (check-before-store, drop, latch -- verified in-tree at `dev_pckbc.c:158-167`). It must NOT fold in, and not merely by the reopening rule: **the restructure makes head==tail <=> empty sound ONLY on the byte path.** The bulk producer at :343-349 compares only against WDC_INBUF_SIZE and can land head exactly on tail with NO WARNING AT ALL (:876-879 mirrors it on tail). *pckbc had ONE producer; wdc has THREE.* A byte-path-only repair ships a half-invariant under a record that reads as soundness. **(3) SEQUENCING: `landiskdisk` SPLITS IN TWO.** The PROBE-level -d attach is part of `wdcflood`'s own witness battery and blocks nothing -- verified: :583 is unreachable without a disk (:461-468 early-returns), so the opus flood measurement necessarily ran disk-attached and the route is already proven. The BATTERY-RIG integration -- the half carrying the 28-34% NINSTRS poison -- is an independent deliverable and NOT a blocker. **The primed-head/tail row is a RUNG-1 DETECTOR row and cannot discharge :145's witness**; the 513-IDENTIFY route can, and was verified sound: no ring reset exists at command start (the only head/tail writes are :143, :165, :347-349, :876-879), IDENTIFY feeds wdc_addtoinbuf 512 bytes per command (:525-533), and 513 x 512 = 262,656 = WDC_INBUF_SIZE exactly. **(4) THE REPETITION RULE: DO NOT MINT, and my dichotomy was wrong on BOTH horns.** Clause (a) does NOT cover it -- (a) is DETECTOR-level and the defect is ROW-level: a one-off row at a latched site prints one line pre-fix and one line post-fix, colourless in both worlds, so it contributes nothing to (a) and hides behind rows that do. **But no new clause is needed, because clause (d) already forces it mechanically:** the fix adds six latch predicates, (d)-DEPENDS-ON mandates a null-repair mutant per predicate (flag never set), and the only row shape that reddens a nulled latch is one firing the same site twice with an EXACT count. Codex's sentence is the row-construction corollary of (d) for the latch class -- the same relation the accept-row failability rule bears to the de-escalation clause. Two overlapping statements of one rule is what the carrier refuses by name. **Disposition: one derivation sentence in the round block, not a carrier clause.** If a future latch round ships a SURVIVING one-off row, that measured escape is the (f)-style warrant to mint. **REFINEMENT ON THE ROWS (minimax): repetition with a "<= 1 line" oracle passes a mutant that prints ZERO. The oracle must be EXACTLY ONE, THEN ZERO** -- announcement AND suppression, which is the pair a latch actually promises.  *** PASS 2 (panel_20260825_204943) FOUND THREE ESCAPES AGAINST A DETECTOR MEASURED 14/14, AND ONE OF THEM IS A STRUCTURAL BLINDNESS OF THE ROWS RATHER THAN A GAP IN THEM. *** All three are L1 -- pre-ship construction, fixed in-round, not filed. **(1) glm -- THE RESET-ON-NORMAL-OPERATION ESCAPE, and it is the sharpest.** ONE line, reusing the existing flag, guard and branch, added inside an existing case for a VALID command: `d->warned_unimpl_cmd = 0;`. **Every site row fires its site TWICE IN SUCCESSION with no normal device operation between**, so the flag is never reset between fires and the row stays green -- while a real guest that probes an unimplemented opcode, issues IDENTIFY, probes again, issues IDENTIFY, floods forever. The same one-line trick applies at every one of the six sites. *This is the `#463` distinctness-invariance finding wearing new clothes: rows that test a property back-to-back are invariant under any edit that only changes what happens BETWEEN the two fires.* **(2) agy -- THE COVERAGE CENSUS, CONFIRMED AGAINST MY OWN PROBE.** "The detector's six site rows do not test six distinct C sites": `:145` has **ZERO** rows while its sibling `:160` has two, and `:583` has three. Also **the non-byte rows probe 16-bit ONLY** -- `mov.w` at both :607 and :1025, never `mov.l`, so a `len != 1` guard narrowed to `len == 2` would escape. **(3) deepseek -- `d->warned_X = !d->warned_X;`**, claimed to toggle so that fires 1 and 3 print while the detector only fires twice. **READING SAYS THIS DOES NOT WORK** -- the assignment sits INSIDE the guard (`if (!d->warned_unimpl_cmd) { d->warned_unimpl_cmd = 1; ...}`), so fire 2 never enters and the toggle never runs. **RECORDED AS A PREDICTION TO BE MEASURED, NOT AS REFUTED** -- this project settles disagreements by measurement, and the seat may be modelling a placement I have not considered. It goes in the second table either way, because the row that would kill it kills a whole CLASS. *** THE ROWS OWED, AND THE THIRD IS THE GENERAL ONE: *** `interleave` -- fire the site, issue a VALID command (0xEC IDENTIFY), fire again, demand ONE line; this is what kills glm's escape. `w32`/`r32` -- 32-bit non-byte access at :607 and :1025, closing agy's width gap. **`fire3` -- fire ONE site THREE times and demand exactly one line**, which kills the toggle class and any period-N latch at once, and is the cheapest row of the three. `:145` remains DISCLOSED-NOT-COVERED in the contract; agy's point stands but the contract already says so. *** AND AN HONEST RECORD ABOUT PROCESS: THE CARRIER'S PRE-TABLE CHECK WOULD HAVE CAUGHT agy's FINDING AND I DID NOT RUN IT. *** Its FIRST item is SIBLING PARITY -- *for each arm the diff touches, compare its observable channels against its nearest sibling arm; an asymmetry is a row you owe*. `:145` with zero rows beside `:160` with two IS that asymmetry, visible by counting, before any mutant was built. The check exists precisely because a table re-run is expensive, and this round is now paying that cost: the first table was measured against a 14-row detector and adding rows changes other mutants' scores, so a SECOND table is owed. **The check costs three greps and about thirty minutes; skipping it cost a table.**  *** THE FULL PASS-2 PANEL (8 of 8 answering; the kimi CLI walled and COVERED BY ITS SUBSTITUTE -- panel.sh reported that correctly for the first time) FOUND AN L2 FLOOR BREACH, TWO WRONG RECORDS IN SHIPPED TEXT, AND A DESIGN CLAIM WITH NO ROW BEHIND IT. *** **(L2 -- FLOOR BREACH, clause (b), grok) `:145` HAS NO DETECTOR ROW, SO THE FIX HAS SIX FIXED SITES AND THE DETECTOR SEES FIVE.** Clause (b) requires failure on a verbatim reinstatement at EVERY fixed site; reinstating `:145`'s unlatched form escapes clean. grok's verdict was DO-NOT-SHIP-AS-A-SIX-SITE-FLOOR and it is right. **Confirmed by counting my own probe: the six site-x2 rows cover FIVE sites -- `P_OVERRUN` appears only in `disjoint`, which fires an unimplemented command and never touches the ring.** The 8/14 -> 14/14 colour change is five tested sites plus `unimpl 2op`. Fix in-round, however late: either add a `:145` row or narrow the fix to five sites. **(L4 -- WRONG RECORD IN SHIPPED PROBE TEXT, codex and grok independently) THE HEADER CONTRADICTS ITS OWN CONTRACT.** It claims to catch *removal of any of the six per-instance latch guards* while the contract eight lines below excludes `:145`. It catches FIVE unique sites. **(L4 -- `disjoint` PROVES LESS THAN ITS NAME, codex.** It exercises only the unimplemented-command transcript, so it proves THAT stimulus matches one regex -- not that all six patterns map uniquely. The row's note overstates it. *** (DESIGN CLAIM WITH NO ROW, codex -- and this is the one I would have missed for good.) 14/14 DOES NOT ENFORCE SIX INDEPENDENT FLAGS. *** Every site test starts a NEW emulator (15 `session()` calls), so **pairing the read/write width flags, or the two ring flags, would pass every isolated row -- as would a PROCESS-GLOBAL latch**, unless one session exercises two controller instances. The round's headline design decision -- six flags, not four -- is therefore UNMEASURED by its own detector. codex adds the mitigating half, checked: the implementation does use six separately initialised per-instance fields, `DEVINIT(wdc)` zeroes the whole allocation, and none is reset or aliased later. **So the CODE is right and the DETECTOR cannot prove it** -- which under clause (e) must be disclosed, not claimed. **(ESCAPE, codex) An inserted `return 1;` immediately after the non-byte-read `fatal()`** leaves the FIRST 16-bit read's buffer untouched while the second runs normally -- and `r16 x2` checks only the line count. Checked by reading: the only `memset(d, 0, sizeof(struct wdc_data))` is at :1126, immediately after the malloc at :1125 in DEVINIT. `COMMAND_RESET` (:484) and `ATAPI_SOFT_RESET` (:601) exist and neither re-zeroes the struct. **A real question, cheaply settled, and worth recording as a negative result so nobody re-asks it.** **(RECORDS, minimax) MY OWN BRIEF'S ROW ARITHMETIC DID NOT ADD UP:** it enumerated 2 controls + 6 site + 3 accept + 1 disjoint = 12 against a stated 14. The two unstated rows are the side-effect rows `abrt 2nd` and `overread -1` -- which are the most interesting rows in the file and the brief left them out of its own census. **(CHALLENGE, minimax) `fatal()` RETURNING IS ASSUMED IN THE :1025 COMMENT, AND "no early-out" DOES NOT ESTABLISH IT** -- no-early-out is about verbosity, not program lifetime. The claim is true and this project settled it on 2026-08-21 by reading `core/debugmsg.c:384-390`, but the comment should CITE that rather than lean on the adjacent no-early-out fact. A fair catch. **(USEFUL FOR `wdcringambig`, ollama_kimi) A WASTE-ONE-SLOT DISAMBIGUATOR IS NOT FORBIDDEN BY CAPACITY:** 512 x 512 = 262,144 usable is still <= 262,655, so a max-length sector transfer still fits. Only the 513-undrained-IDENTIFY fill exceeds it. **Any future claim that "waste-one breaks the exact-fit sizing" is wrong**, and that is worth carrying to the ring round before it invents the objection.  *** KILL TABLE 1 -- 8 MUTANTS AGAINST THE 14-ROW DETECTOR, AND ONE ESCAPED. *** Preserved at `regress/artifacts/wdcflood/table1_14rows/` (12 files + a README stating what the numbers mean and why the directory is stamped). Tree restored and cmp-verified against SEC, sentinel cleared, zero live processes. SCORES, every reddened row re-extracted with an ANCHORED trailing-`FAIL` match: `base` 14/14 (identity -- the harness scores the unmutated copy exactly as SEC does); `Mb1` 12/14 delete the :583 guard -> `unimpl x2`, `unimpl 2op`; `M1` 12/14 null the repair, flag never set -> same two; `M2` 11/14 SET BEFORE ANNOUNCE, zero lines -> those two plus `disjoint`; `M3` 13/14 last-warned-opcode -> **`unimpl 2op` ALONE**; `M4` 13/14 ABRT moved inside the guard -> **`abrt 2nd` ALONE**; `M5` 13/14 `return -1` moved inside the guard -> **`overread -1` ALONE**; `M6` **14/14 -- ESCAPED, ZERO ROWS REDDENED**. *** THE THREE SINGLE-ROW KILLS ARE THE USEFUL RESULT, NOT THE SCORES. *** `M3`, `M4` and `M5` each redden exactly ONE row, and those three rows exist for exactly those escapes -- nothing else in the file covers them. `abrt 2nd` and `overread -1` are the two rows that read a guest-visible SIDE EFFECT rather than a line count, and they are the only rows that can see a repair swallowed by a guard. *** M2 IS THE MEASURED VINDICATION OF AN ORACLE CHOICE. *** It sets the flag before the test so the site emits ZERO lines. **A `<= 1 line` oracle would have passed it**; `exactly 1` catches it. That choice was argued from a seat's reasoning and is now measured. *** AND M6 IS THE ESCAPE, PREDICTED BY A SEAT ON PASS 2 AND CONFIRMED HERE. *** It swaps the latch operand for the GUEST-RESETTABLE `d->seccnt`: `if (len != 1 && !d->seccnt) { d->seccnt = 1; fatal(...); }`. Every row in table 1 fires its site TWICE IN SUCCESSION, so nothing between the fires ever puts the operand back and the mutant looks perfectly latched. A guest that writes `seccnt = 0` between wide writes floods without bound. **This is a STRUCTURAL blindness of the row design, not a missing mutant** -- the same shape as `#463`'s distinctness invariance, where rows that assert a property back-to-back cannot see an edit that changes only what happens BETWEEN the assertions. *** DETECTOR NOW 22 ROWS, MEASURED 22/22 ON THE FIXED BUILD (`table2_22rows/base_22rows.raw`). *** Seven rows added, each closing something table 1 or pass 2 exposed: `overrun x2` (the :145 row -- **this is what closes the L2 floor breach**, and it needed a hardware loop, `dt r3` / `bf` with a computed displacement, because 513 undrained IDENTIFYs unrolled would be 513 debugger commands); `interleave` (fire, VALID command, fire); `w16 reset` (fire, guest CLEARS the operand, fire -- the M6 killer); `fire3` (kills period-N latches, not just period-2); `w32 x2` and `r32 x2` (the width rows probed 16-bit only, so a guard narrowed to `len == 2` escaped); `r16 value` and `w16 value` (value oracles at the two width sites, for a `return` inserted after a latched `fatal()` -- which a count-only row cannot see). Row hygiene checked: no name over 13 chars, no duplicates, no name that is a prefix of another followed by a space. TABLE 2 is running against the 22-row detector with three mutants table 1 could not have had: `Mb2` removes the :145 guard verbatim (the clause-(b) reinstatement at the site that had no row), `M7` is the reset-on-normal-operation escape, `M8` is the period-2 latch. All three anchors were verified to occur EXACTLY ONCE in the source first -- **a mutant that fails to apply scores a false clean**, which is the worst possible failure for a kill table. *** A CAPTION DEFECT IN THE APPARATUS, FOUND AND FIXED AT SOURCE. *** `killwdc.sh` wrote its header at start with the row count and the pre-fix score as LITERALS (`14 rows`, `8/14`). The moment pass 2 forced seven more rows, table 2's own header became wrong about its own size. The script now DERIVES the count (`grep -c '^row(' ...`) and stamps a UTC start time instead of quoting scores it cannot know. Table 2's already-written header is stale and is corrected in place; the script fix stops it recurring. *A table that misreports its own size cannot be cited safely at all.*  *** KILL TABLE 2 IS CLEAN: 22-ROW DETECTOR, TEN MUTANTS, **ZERO ESCAPES**, EVERY LOG INTERNALLY CONSISTENT. *** Preserved at `regress/artifacts/wdcflood/table2_22rows/` with a header that DERIVES its row count rather than quoting one. Tree restored and cmp-verified against SEC, sentinel cleared, zero live processes. base 22/22; Mb1 18/22; M1 18/22; M2 17/22; M3 21/22; M4 21/22; M5 21/22; M6 21/22; M7 21/22; M8 21/22; Mb2 21/22. **Consistency check on all eleven logs: score + anchored-red count == 22 in every one**, which is the check that would catch a contaminated extractor. *** SIX ESCAPES, SIX SINGLE-ROW KILLS, EACH BY THE ROW BUILT FOR IT -- and that one-to-one correspondence is the result, not the scores: *** M3 last-warned-opcode -> `unimpl 2op` ALONE; M4 ABRT inside the guard -> `abrt 2nd` ALONE; M5 `return -1` inside the guard -> `overread -1` ALONE; M6 guest-resettable operand -> `w16 reset` ALONE; M7 reset-on-normal-operation -> `interleave` ALONE; Mb2 the :145 verbatim reinstatement -> `overrun x2` ALONE. **Nothing else in the file sees any of them.** *** THE L2 FLOOR BREACH IS CLOSED BY MEASUREMENT. *** `Mb2` is the exact edit that swept CLEAN against the 14-row detector -- removing :145's guard verbatim -- and it now reddens `overrun x2`, the row that did not exist when the breach was found. Clause (b) holds at all six fixed sites. *** M8 VINDICATES A CAUTION, AND THE CAUTION IS THE TRANSFERABLE PART. *** deepseek proposed `d->warned_X = !d->warned_X;` as a period-2 escape. I read its SPECIFIC edit as unworkable -- the assignment sits INSIDE the guard, so fire 2 never reaches it -- and recorded it as **"a prediction to be MEASURED, not refuted"**. M8 constructs the same class differently (toggle BEFORE the guard) and escapes a two-fire oracle exactly as deepseek said the class would. **Wrong about the placement, RIGHT ABOUT THE CLASS.** Declaring it refuted on the strength of a correct reading of one construction would have lost a real escape. *A seat can be wrong about the mechanism and right about the family; the family is the part worth building a row for.* *** CLAUSE (c), THE NULL MEDIUM, IS NOW MEASURED AND IN ITS STRONGEST FORM: 0/22 ON BOTH. *** `nullmedium_absent.raw` (a binary that does not exist) and `nullmedium_notanemu.raw` (a real executable that is not an emulator) each score **0/22 -- every row fails, not merely some**. It had NOT been verified before; the question was raised against the round's own readiness and answered in seconds. **AND THE MEASUREMENT EXPOSED A DESIGN PROPERTY THAT WAS ACCIDENTAL RATHER THAN INTENDED:** the three accept rows expect ZERO diagnostics, so a naive implementation would PASS against silence -- zero is exactly what silence produces. They fail correctly only because `n()` returns `"died"` rather than `"0"` when the run produced nothing (probe :227-228). **That single line is what stops every accept row in this file from being vacuous under clause (c)**, and it was not written for that reason. Worth carrying to any future detector with absence-shaped oracles: an "expect 0" row MUST distinguish 'ran and saw nothing' from 'did not run'.  *** THE READINESS ADJUDICATION RETURNED **HOLD-FOR** AND FOUND TWO SHIPPED ROWS VACUOUS. ASKING BEFORE THE TABLE FINISHED IS WHAT MADE THAT POSSIBLE -- a clean sweep invites ratification. *** **`r16 value` WAS VACUOUS AS BUILT.** Its oracle was `printed(t,"r2") != "absent"` against a wanted `"read"`, so it passed whenever the debugger echoed ANY hex value -- structurally incapable of failing while the emulator lived. **Confirmed: green under every one of table 2's ten mutants -- it did not exist for table 1, which measured a 14-row detector, and an earlier note said 'tables 1 and 2', which is false.** The `live` control already covered session death, so the row measured nothing at all. **AND BOTH WIDTH VALUE ROWS CHECKED THE WRONG FIRE.** The escape they cite -- a `return` inserted after a latched `fatal()` -- corrupts the FIRST access (flag unset, guard entered, return skips the repair); the SECOND finds the flag set, skips the guard and repairs normally. Both rows read the value ONCE, after both fires, and so saw a perfectly good value. The contract line claiming they carried value oracles "for exactly that edit" was FALSE AS BUILT. Repaired to check BOTH fires, with a low-byte mask because the repair sets only `data[0]` and asserting the upper byte would make the row about the wrong thing. *** TABLE 3 EARNS THE REPAIRED ROWS THEIR MEASURED KILL, WHICH IS WHAT A REPAIRED ROW OWES: *** `table3_repaired/`, base 22/22. `Mv1` (delete `idata = data[0]`, the write-side repair) 18/22 -> r16 value, w16 value, overrun x2, accept ec. `Mv2` (delete `data[0] = odata`, the read-side repair inside the `ret:` tail) 18/22 -> devsig, abrt 2nd, r16 value, w16 value. **`Mv3` (codex's EXACT edit -- insert `return 1;` after the latched READ `fatal()`) 21/22 -> `r16 value` ALONE.** *** Mv3 IS THE ONE THAT PROVES THE REPAIR RATHER THAN THE ROW. *** It corrupts only the first access, so **the ORIGINAL one-value form would have scored 22/22 against it** -- the escape would have shipped invisibly behind a row whose whole stated purpose was to catch it. One row in twenty-two sees it, and it is the repaired one. COLLATERAL WORTH READING RATHER THAN DISMISSING: `Mv2` reddens `devsig`, because deleting `data[0] = odata` breaks the status read the device-signature control depends on. rows.note: *** CLOSED 2026-08-30 AS ALREADY FIXED.  The row says `selfmutant.py has NO TIMEOUT: a hanging mutant wedges gate 2`.  It has TWO, and they are enforced. ***  `BUILD_TIMEOUT` (120 s) and `RUN_TIMEOUT` (60 s), both overridable by environment, are passed to a `run_bounded()` helper at the build and run call sites.  **VERIFIED AS ENFORCED RATHER THAN MERELY PRESENT**, because this project's own recurring defect is a value that exists and is never used -- `kill495.sh` computes `WORDS_OK` and references it nowhere, and `panel.sh` printed 're-firing once' and re-fired nothing.  Here the chain is complete: `communicate(timeout=)`, then `os.killpg(os.getpgid(p.pid), SIGKILL)` on timeout, then a bounded drain, then a descriptive failure string.  *** AND THE `killpg` IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART, not the timeout value. ***  The file's own comment records why: *a bare `subprocess.run(timeout=)` kills only the DIRECT child*, so on the `gcc -> cc1` shape the grandchild survives and the gate still wedges.  Killing the process GROUP is what actually closes the hang.  It also records a reviewing seat's prediction that the post-kill drain would block forever, and that the prediction was tested rather than accepted.  The comment block also names the tuning hazard honestly: a too-tight timeout turns a busy host into a red gate, which is why both values are environment-overridable rather than literals.  *Found while auditing rows with empty ledger notes.  Of 87 such open rows, 85 are documented in OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md and only two were undocumented anywhere -- this was one, and reading it to write it up is what showed it was stale.  The empty field was schema redundancy; the stale STATE was the real defect, and only opening the source found it.*

rows.title: smnotland  selfmutant.py never verifies the mutation LANDED in the tree it compiled -- the missing postcondition behind all three recorded hazards

entries.note: MEASURED: a subject outside the mirrored src/ passes the anchor check, lands in NEITHER arm, and the helper prints 'mutant applied but the detector did NOT report a failure' -- both halves false. This UNIFIES the three separately-recorded extra-flags hazards (omitted flags that fail to link; flags making both arms consistently wrong; an absolute path compiling the pristine subject into both arms) as instances of ONE missing postcondition. Fix: after link_tree, require tree/<subject> to be a regular non-symlink file containing `new` exactly once in the mutant arm and `old` exactly once in the pristine arm. Also covers the DrvFs case-slip variant.

*** THE SEAT THAT BUILT THE ANSWER. ***  It CONSTRUCTED THREE ESCAPES and measured each against both the shipped helper and my proposed fix. E1 `old == new` -- a two-file copy, ZERO characters of difference -- is the smallest apparatus failure there is and produced the identical false sentence. E2 `new` = `old` + a trailing comment: lands, compiles, inert. E3 EXTRA_FLAGS naming the subject by ABSOLUTE path: the mutant text DOES land in the tree, so no tree-file postcondition can see it -- and gate_offline.sh:955-963 already calls that 'the dangerous one of the three', which makes the filing's 'unifies the three extra-flags hazards' claim MEASURABLY FALSE. Its answer: compare what the COMPILER PRODUCED, not what the harness wrote -- mutant differs from pristine 12/12, the three escapes byte-identical, 0.048 ms of sha256 against a 1370 ms build. *** AND IT FOUND THE ONE THING THAT WOULD HAVE SHIPPED A VACUOUS CONTROL: with -g or -g3 the PRISTINE arm's binary DIFFERS FROM ITSELF across two tree paths, so binary identity would silently stop firing rather than go red. Re-measured here and confirmed exactly -- and the remedy (build both arms at ONE path) verified: -g3 pristine-vs-pristine IDENTICAL, mutant still differs. *** It derived the timeouts from measurement (slowest build 1.37 s, slowest run 0.31 s), measured the process-group kill (child pgid 32 vs the gate's 11, so killpg provably cannot reach the gate), found three MORE no-token paths, and BUILT A WORKING PROTOTYPE it validated at 12/12.

FLAGSHIP RECORDS AND DOCTRINE SEAT. Badge s. *** IT RULED AGAINST THE ROUND'S OWN SCOPE and the ruling was accepted: *** applying the reopening rule prong by prong, smhang needs a WALL-CLOCK ORACLE, so the 'same detector, no new oracle' prong fails objectively -- and the ledger's grouping argument ('both fixes are a dozen lines together') is a SIZE argument, which is not one of the rule's prongs. It also named a real doctrine gap: the reopening rule was written for emulator sites and it is undecided whether it governs apparatus rounds at all. On the witness ladder it ruled that none of the four values fits an apparatus round and proposed extending the vocabulary today while the ladder is still forward-only. It found TWO WRONG RECORDS IN MY OWN BRIEF -- a '9-line block replaced by a 1-line body' pair that DOES NOT EXIST (the largest is diskimage_io, 4 lines -> 2; my number came from a scratchpad mutant), and a 'verbatim' source quote that had silently dropped the `try:` and so hid the finally/rmtree path the timeout design depends on. Both corrected in the brief. It independently confirmed diskimage_io breaks the fragment count, and VERIFIED selfcheckman is already fixed by 7e3b120. *** ONE CALL OVERTURNED BY MEASUREMENT: it predicted run(timeout=)'s post-kill DRAIN would block forever on the grandchild's pipe. False on POSIX -- CPython calls process.wait() there, not communicate(). Its CONCLUSION survived anyway, for a different reason: run() leaves TWO ORPHANS spinning where killpg leaves zero. ***

46 KB, and it found a hazard NOBODY ELSE DID: a harness in a symlinked SUBDIRECTORY of regress/. link_tree symlinks any directory not containing real_file, and the kernel resolves `sub/../../src/...` by following `sub` FIRST, landing outside the tree. No seat stated that. *** LATENT, not live -- every harness is a flat regress/diff_*.c today. It converged unprompted on whole-file equality and on mirroring directories for real. entries.ev: read of regress/selfmutant.py at c125450 -- a READING, not a run
entries.note: **Both checks are LIVE EXECUTABLE CODE, verified by reading the file rather than its comments.**  (3c) reads the subject back from the tree that gets compiled and compares it to the exact text this helper wrote, `return 1` on mismatch.  (7) compares the two arms' binary digests and `return 1`s if they are identical.  Both print `SELFMUTANT_SETUP`, a token DISTINCT from a detector verdict -- so a setup fault can never be read as a result about the detector, which is the whole point.  **And (7) is not redundant with (3c), which is the part worth keeping.**  The source records three escapes CONSTRUCTED AND MEASURED that pass a tree-file postcondition and still print the false *the detector did NOT report a failure*: a mutant that is `old` plus a trailing comment; a mutation inside a section `--gc-sections` discards; and the one the tree check structurally cannot see -- extra-flags naming the subject by an ABSOLUTE path, so the REPO copy is compiled while the tree copy sits there mutated.  A tree postcondition proves what is ON DISK; only the binary proves what the COMPILER CONSUMED.  *** NOT CLOSED, DELIBERATELY.  THIS IS A READING AND THE ROW WANTS A RUN. ***  The source claims 12/12 across the shipped lanes; that is its author's measurement, not mine, and this project's oldest distinction is between a reading and a measurement.  Running `selfmutant.py` is a harness invocation and a nine-seat panel was on the machine, so it was deliberately not run -- load-induced false results have cost this session twice already.  **Close it after a clean run, not before.**

rows.witness: harness:selfmutant.py's own (3c) postcondition -- the arm's subject is read back from the tree that gets compiled and compared against the exact text the helper wrote. `harness:` is the correct witness kind here because the subject of the row IS the test apparatus.
rows.state_note:
*** EVIDENCE 2026-08-27: THE DEFECT WAS REAL AND IS ALREADY FIXED. The row has been sitting OPEN describing a defect that was closed the same day it was assessed. Recommend CLOSE. ***

**The postcondition the row says is missing now exists, and it is stronger than the row asked for.** `regress/selfmutant.py` carries a block headed *(3c) THE MUTATION MUST HAVE LANDED, AND THE TEST IS EXACT TEXT, NOT A FRAGMENT COUNT*:
  * it refuses a subject that is a SYMLINK in the arm tree, saying in as many words that *the mutant would not land*;
  * it writes the one real file in place;
  * **it reads that file back FROM THE TREE IT WILL COMPILE** (`tree_subject`, which sits under the same `tree` the binary is built in) with `newline=""`, and compares the WHOLE TEXT against what the helper computed;
  * a mismatch reports **SETUP**, not FAIL -- an apparatus failure, correctly distinguished from a measurement result.

entries.note: FILED BEFORE rtcdet/rtcgate CLOSE, because rtcdet's own assess note was the ONLY place this design item existed and closing that row would have orphaned it. The item: #429 range-checks a guest rate inside dev_rtc.c, and the filing argued the narrowing should move into the timer core instead, where every device that derives a rate from a guest value would get it. *** THE PREMISE IS STALE AND TWO SEATS MEASURED IT INDEPENDENTLY. *** The filing named dev_footbridge, dev_vr41xx and dev_jazz as unguarded. Read today: dev_jazz.c:432-434 computes 1000.0/(idata+1.0), bounded above by 1000 and bounded BY CONSTRUCTION since b679170 (#257, 2026-07-18); dev_vr41xx.c:604-612 is `int hz = RTCL1_L_HZ / idata` with RTCL1_L_HZ = 0x8000 (vr_rtcreg.h:90), an unsigned divide so hz <= 32768; dev_footbridge derives from emulated_hz over a 32-bit divisor and its +INF path is already fixed. NONE of the three can exceed TIMER_MAX_FREQUENCY. So the wide-domain narrowing case that justified a four-device round does not exist. What IS shared is the OPPOSITE END: all three can land below TIMER_MIN_FREQUENCY, which timer_clamp_freq floors SILENTLY -- timer.c:100-108 sets was_clamped only on the ceiling. That is the real residual and it is a different, smaller item than the one filed. Not yet reproduced; no witness at rung 2-4, so it is a design item, not a fix.

entries.note:
*** DO NOT DROP -- RETITLE. THE ROW'S OWN TITLE IS REFUTED BY MEASUREMENT, AND ITS PROPOSED FIX LOCATION IS THE ONE PLACE THE FIX CANNOT GO. ***

dev_vr41xx.c:606 is `int hz = RTCL1_L_HZ / idata` -- an INTEGER divide with RTCL1_L_HZ = 0x8000. The entire domain idata >= 32769 collapses to hz = 0, which timer_clamp_freq then floors SILENTLY to 1e-8 Hz: one tick per 3.17 years. *** A GUEST ASKING FOR 0.5 Hz GETS A TIMER THAT NEVER FIRES. ***  Not 'lands below the floor' -- destroyed BEFORE timer.c ever sees it. Flooring 0 -> 1e-8 in timer.c is CORRECT; a floor complaint there would make this noisier while still wrong.

RUNG-3 WITNESS BUILT TODAY, two subtypes, unmodified in-tree machine, no device_add, every planted word disassembled and text-compared before stepping:
    hpcmips/z50 (VR4121) cold debugger, no boot
    LIVENESS  idata=0x00008000 -> [ vr41xx: rtc interrupts at 1 Hz ]   control green
    SUBJECT   idata=0x00010000 -> [ vr41xx: rtc interrupts at 0 Hz ]   guest asked 0.5 Hz
Identical on mobilepro770. Both required controls present: liveness AND device signature ((vr41xx@0xb000000)+0xd0 plus the device's own message -- RAM produces no line at all). The encoding guard earned its keep: the first run REFUSED a verdict because the expected mnemonic strings were wrong, and reported SETUP rather than passing.

TWO OTHER LEGS MEASURED, one FALSE: *** footbridge is REFUTED *** -- bounded below by emulated_hz / 2^32, so emulated_hz would have to be < 42.95 Hz; on a 33 MHz machine the worst case is 0.0077 Hz, six orders of magnitude above the floor. The jazz leg is much weaker than filed: 64-bit store only (any 32-bit store bottoms out at 2.33e-7 Hz, 23x above floor).

entries.ev: src/core/debugmsg.c (debug() vs fatal(), read side by side)

entries.note:
*** WORSE THAN FILED, ON TWO MEASUREMENTS -- AND ONE OF THEM REFUTES A CLAIM IN THE TOOL I SHIPPED FOR THIS ROW. ***

(1) THE EMIT PATH AMPLIFIES 161x, MEASURED. va_debug() (debugmsg.c:118-137) emits ONE printf("%c") PER CHARACTER, plus an indent loop printing spaces one at a time. The seat replicated that loop byte-for-byte rather than paraphrasing it and benchmarked against a single fputs, to /dev/null so sink cost is excluded: 0.490 s vs 0.003 s over 200,000 calls on a 62-byte message -- 2.45 us against 0.02 us, AMPLIFICATION 161.2x, and that is a FLOOR because a real line-buffered console is worse. So a flood is not log noise; it is guest-controlled HOST-CPU amplification on a path -q cannot silence.

(2) *** census_floods.py SAYS REACHABILITY 'NEEDS THE CALL GRAPH, AND A TOOL THAT GUESSED WOULD BE WORSE THAN ONE THAT DECLINES'. THAT PREMISE IS FALSE AND I WROTE IT. ***  DEVICE_ACCESS() IS the dispatch entry memory_rw calls, so lexical containment inside its brace-matched body is a SOUND STRUCTURAL OVER-APPROXIMATION -- no call graph required. The seat built it:
    776 fatal() under src/devices/
    475 inside a DEVICE_ACCESS() body            (guest MMIO handler)
    150 inside a switch default: in that body    (unhandled-offset arm)
     10 of those guarded by a latch in their OWN arm
    *** 140 UNLATCHED AT THE SITE, in 53 files ***
POSITIVE CONTROLS BOTH LAND, and it resolves PER-PATH -- the resolution my census says it lacks. It flags dev_rtc.c:168-173 (the two pre-#429 arms this row names), and in dev_wdc.c it correctly SEPARATES :731/:761 (latched by warned_badlen, #337's work) from :583/:1007 (unlatched) -- i.e. it finds the path #337 MISSED inside a file my census scores as 'latched'.

SO THE HONEST HEADLINE IS 140 SITES, NOT 543 CALLS AND NOT 72 FILES. Per-path, actionable, and mechanically re-derivable.

(3) A RUNG-3 WITNESS IS AVAILABLE TODAY AT NEAR-ZERO COST, and the filing seat (me) missed it: regress/pit8253_latch_probe.py is committed and already drives real guest ARM instructions through real address decode to PA 0x7c000040-43 on an unmodified -E cats -- the 8253's own registers -- and dev_8253.c carries unlatched default:-arm fatal() at :158 and :184 (plus :250/:253). ONE MORE ARM on an already-committed probe witnesses an unsuppressable 161x-amplified flood.

(4) DETECTOR, NOT FIX, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL: the round-scope rule takes ONE site, and a second only in the SAME DEVICE. rtcflood and wdcflood are different devices, so THE PROJECT'S OWN SCOPE RULE FORBIDS FIXING THIS CLASS IN ONE ROUND -- 140 sites at one round each is not a plan. What a floodclass round can honestly deliver is the per-path detector plus the ranked list.

HONEST BOUND THE SEAT INSISTED ON, and it is right: the harm is to the HOST (CPU burn, unbounded log growth, unsuppressable), NOT to the emulated guest. floodclass is a host-side denial-of-service surface, not guest corruption. It still outranks the rest of its cluster because the others have no harm of any kind -- theirs is a wrong record.

TWO MORE INSTANCES FOLDED IN RATHER THAN FILED SEPARATELY, on the adjudicator's call that a standalone row for each is the near-duplicate proliferation this row exists to prevent. (1) `asicdefaultflood`: dev_dreamcast_asic.c's default: arm is unlatched -- silent at default verbosity, but under -v a guest scanning the window floods, and the asicbadaddr round routes SIXTY-FOUR more byte offsets into that arm. It rides with that round, whose survival sweep already exercises the arm. (2) `gdromxfrflood`: dev_dreamcast_gdrom.c's `Transfering %i bytes` fatal is NOT latched, so a guest looping legal DMA floods host stderr -- while the two ILLEGAL paths #462 latched stay quiet. That inversion sits three lines from a new comment arguing flooding is what every latch here exists to prevent. Pre-existing, but #462 touched the line.

rows.title: pitflip  The 8253's 16-bit LSB/MSB selector is one-way, so it manufactures a count of 0 and silently loses bytes

closure.note:

What should be weighed against that is that the round SHIPPED A MECHANISM WITH NO COVERAGE and pass 2 caught it -- the control-word rewind had zero rows until R10/R11, and two independent seats produced the same one-line mutant that passed everything. The round had ALSO run no panel at all until pass 2, which the implementing seat disclosed itself.

entries.note: MEASURED at rung 3. dev_8253.c:170-171 CLEARS I8253_TIMER_LSB and nothing ever sets it back; a real 8254's flip-flop ALTERNATES on every access. entries.note:
*** THE FACT THAT DECIDES WHAT THIS ROUND CAN HONESTLY DO: THERE IS NO RUNNING COUNT. ***  Found while writing the design brief. d->counter[3] is WRITTEN only in the mode-write path and READ only in the counter-read path -- IT NEVER DECREMENTS. timer0_tick() increments pending_interrupts_timer0 and touches nothing else. The file's own header carries the author's TODO at line 35: '(Split counter[] into reset value and current value.)'

So d->counter[] is the PROGRAMMED RELOAD VALUE, FROZEN. gxemul models the timer's RATE (timer_add / timer_update_frequency) and its INTERRUPTS, but never a counting register.

WHY THAT REFRAMES THE FIX: OpenBSD's microtime() latches and reads the counter to INTERPOLATE SUB-TICK TIME. If a 'correct' latch returns a constant, the guest's interpolated time does not advance within a tick -- a different wrong answer from 0, and arguably a WORSE one because it is plausible rather than obviously broken. So the candidate that looks most correct (return the programmed value) may be the one that misleads a guest furthest, and the honest round may be smaller than the row implies: make the latch not-an-error and not-a-flood, and DOCUMENT that sub-tick interpolation is unmodelled. The panel was asked exactly that, and asked to say so if this is a DOCUMENT round wearing a FIX round's clothes.

*** THE DRIVING SEAT REFUSED THE PANEL'S DESIGN AND MEASURED WHY. ***  Four of six seats converged on 'make the latch non-clobbering and non-fatal, RETURN THE RELOAD VALUE, and document that it is not a live count'. The seat BUILT that as candidate C1 and measured it causing a GUEST DIVIDE-BY-ZERO: OpenBSD's findcpuspeed() (_guest-src-openbsd22/.../clock.c:333-344) programs the counter to 0xffff and divides by (0xffff - gettick()); under C1 gettick() returns 0xffff, so the divisor is 0.

AND C1 DID NOT EVEN DELIVER WHAT IT PROMISED: it returned the HIGH BYTE TWICE (0x2e2e, not the reload 0x2e9c), because pitflip leaves the LSB/MSB selector stuck at MSB. The 'return the reload value' option does not return the reload value.

*** THE SEAT-CLASS DOCTRINE DECIDED IT, NOT THE COUNT. ***  The three seats voting for the reload value were the PACKET-FED Ollama seats, which PIPELINE.md says are never equivalent votes on repo fact. BOTH FILE-READING seats that answered (agy, grok) warned against it, and kimi flagged the same hazard class. Codex was a SEAT FAILURE at that panel, not agreement. A 4-2 count concealed a 0-2 split among the seats that could open the file.

entries.note:
PASS 2 ON #439 -- 7 OF 7 SCRIPTABLE SEATS, THE FIRST FULL SCRIPTABLE PANEL OF THIS CAMPAIGN. Codex answered for real (20,699 bytes) after ten consecutive echo-only walls.

*** SIX SEATS SOUND; CODEX DEFECTIVE -- AND CODEX WAS RIGHT. ***  'The latch is never consumed, so the selected counter returns zero indefinitely.' Verified in source: latched[] is SET at :212, cleared ONLY at :219 by a non-latch mode write, and NEVER cleared by the read at :163. After one latch command, every subsequent read of that counter returns 0 until the guest happens to rewrite the mode byte. A real 8254 CONSUMES the latch per the programmed RW format.

The seat that had been WALLED for the pass-1 panel is the one that found it, which is the clearest argument this campaign has produced for discharging a wall rather than recording it and moving on. glm gestured at the same thing ('the sticky latch').

NOT A REGRESSION: pre-#439 a latch clobbered mode_byte and subsequent reads also fell to the default arm returning 0, plus an unsilenceable flood. But it is a real defect in the fix, and SHIP-WITH-FIX is this project's practice on a pass-2 finding.

HANDED TO THE IN-FLIGHT pitflip ROUND rather than fixed separately, and the reason is technical not merely practical: the consume semantics INTERACT WITH THE LSB/MSB FLIP-FLOP. In 16-bit mode a real latch delivers TWO bytes before reverting -- and the selector is exactly what pitflip is fixing. Two rounds editing dev_8253.c at once would also contend.

THE REFUSAL OF THE PASS-1 MAJORITY IS VINDICATED. The six SOUND verdicts converged on the brief's substantive question -- agy: 'returning 0 avoids guest kernel divide-by-zero crashes, preserves programmed mode state'; deepseek: 'the least harmful of three wrong answers and not a guest-visible regression'; minimax: 'the write-side fix matches the 8254 and removes a real bug'. *** A CORRECTION TO A CORRECTION, IN THE DIRECTION THAT UNDERSTATES REACHABILITY. ***  #439 recorded as MEASURED FALSE that 'the guest function is gettick(), not microtime()'. MEASURED: TIMER_LATCH is issued in TWO places -- sys/arch/i386/isa/clock.c:207 (in gettick()) AND sys/arch/i386/i386/microtime.s:58 (in microtime, which then reads LSB/MSB back and consults the 8259 IRR). The original filing's LINE CITATION was gettick's body and its FUNCTION NAME was microtime's, so the claim is only HALF false -- and the half that was wrong made the defect look less reachable than it is.

This project's own rule -- grep for the siblings before calling it fixed -- applied to a CORRECTION rather than a fix. I did not do that when I recorded it.

The #439 refusal itself is independently confirmed from the guest source: clock.c:331-344 programs the reload to 0xffff and divides by (0xffff - gettick()), so C1 returning the reload gives divisor exactly 0 and a #DE. The refusal's premise holds; it was not a judgement call.

MEASURED (build/gxemul, -v -v -V -T -E cats -M 32): device order is 8259 @0x7c000020, 8259 @0x7c0000a0, *** 8253 @0x7c000040 ADDED AFTER BOTH PICs, *** pccmos @0x7c000070. The pointer copy sits at bus_isa.c:224-225, between the first device_add (:223) and the second (:235); the 8253's device_add is at :244. Construction order confirmed in the RUNNING PROGRAM, not inferred -- and it independently confirms the 0x7c000040 mapping.

MEASURED (grep census): pending_timer_interrupts has exactly ONE writer (dev_8253.c:282) and TWO pointer-cachers (bus_isa.c:225, dev_v3.c:298), both caching before their 8253 can exist.

*** MEASURED, AND THIS IS THE PART NOBODY STATED: dev_8253.c contains ZERO decrements of pending_interrupts_timer0. ***  Every other timer device in the tree drains its own counter from inside its own DEVICE_ACCESS handler -- dev_jazz.c:423,443, dev_luna88k.c:800, dev_mc146818.c:563, dev_vr41xx.c:634, dev_footbridge.c:583,594-595. The 8253 ALONE outsourced its drain to bus_isa.c:134-138.

READ: that drain is unreachable for TWO INDEPENDENT reasons, *** so moving the pointer copy after device_add -- the fix as filed -- changes NOTHING observable: *** (1) nothing ever calls isa_interrupt_deassert for line 0, as dev_8253.c has no INTERRUPT_DEASSERT; and (2) dev_8259.c clears irr DIRECTLY on EOI (:107, :122), bypassing the isa deassert handler entirely.

REFILE AS: 'the 8253's pending-interrupt counter has no reachable drain -- it is the only timer device in the tree that cannot ack', grade DESIGN + needs-witness. Consequence (READ): once any guest touches the PIT, in_use goes 1, the counter rises monotonically and never drains, so DEVICE_TICK re-asserts isa.0 on EVERY device tick (TICK_SHIFT 14) rather than at the programmed rate.

TWO THINGS THE FILING SEAT MISSED: dev_v3.c:298 is not merely 'the same shape' -- it is the same bug for the same reason needing the same two-part fix; and if a machine ever created two ISA buses (bus_pci.c calls bus_isa_init at :476 and :1060), the second copy would be NON-NULL AND ALIAS THE FIRST BUS'S 8253 -- worse than NULL, and silent.

THE WITNESS THAT WOULD SETTLE IT, rung 3 on -E cats: program counter 0 to ~18 Hz, free-run 200 ms, read the 8259 IRR (expect bit0), write specific-EOI 0x60 to 0x7c000020, free-run ~5 ms, read IRR again. Draining correctly => 0 (next tick due at ~55 ms); no drain => 1 again on the very next device tick. Clean discriminator, no source change.

rows.state_note:
*** EVIDENCE 2026-08-27: TRUE structurally, but LATENT -- no guest-visible channel exists today, so it cannot be witnessed or detected without changing the code first. ***

**True:** `bus_isa` copies a pointer before the device that sets it has been added, so `d->ptr_to_pending_timer_interrupts` is NULL afterwards.

**But nothing dereferences it.** The consumer is the ISA-device deassert of line 0 -- the `... & 1 && !(irr & 1)` test -- **which never happens**. Programming the PIT (guest I/O sets `in_use=1`) reaches the ticks and the IRQ 0 *assert*, but never that decrement path.

> **So a detector row is impossible without a product change**, and a fix on its own is unobservable. That is the definition of dormant defensive debt, and it ranks below every guest-reachable row.

*** THE FIX IDIOM IS FIFTEEN LINES ABOVE, IN THE SAME FUNCTION. *** `pic1` is taken from `device_add`'s return value -- i.e. after the device exists -- which is exactly the ordering this pointer copy fails to observe. A transferred warrant, and a cheap one.

*A seat also noted the contrast worth keeping: elsewhere (mc146818) the same-class pending ack is done LOCALLY -- the device decrements its own counter on the guest ack and deasserts there -- rather than through a copied pointer. The copied-pointer shape is the outlier.*

entries.note:
*** THE DRIVING SEAT REFUSED THE PANEL'S DESIGN AND MEASURED WHY. ***  Four of six seats converged on 'make the latch non-clobbering and non-fatal, RETURN THE RELOAD VALUE, and document that it is not a live count'. The seat BUILT that as candidate C1 and measured it causing a GUEST DIVIDE-BY-ZERO: OpenBSD's findcpuspeed() (_guest-src-openbsd22/.../clock.c:333-344) programs the counter to 0xffff and divides by (0xffff - gettick()); under C1 gettick() returns 0xffff, so the divisor is 0.

AND C1 DID NOT EVEN DELIVER WHAT IT PROMISED: it returned the HIGH BYTE TWICE (0x2e2e, not the reload 0x2e9c), because pitflip leaves the LSB/MSB selector stuck at MSB. The 'return the reload value' option does not return the reload value.

*** THE SEAT-CLASS DOCTRINE DECIDED IT, NOT THE COUNT. ***  The three seats voting for the reload value were the PACKET-FED Ollama seats, which PIPELINE.md says are never equivalent votes on repo fact. BOTH FILE-READING seats that answered (agy, grok) warned against it, and kimi flagged the same hazard class. Codex was a SEAT FAILURE at that panel, not agreement. A 4-2 count concealed a 0-2 split among the seats that could open the file.

WHAT SHIPPED (#439): the latch is ACCEPTED, latches NOTHING, and disturbs NO state -- a latched[3] flag, a write-arm branch returning before it touches mode_byte/mode[], and a read-arm branch returning 0 with the limitation documented in the code and in the file header. Guest-visible values are unchanged from the committed build, so it cannot regress anything. pitclobber travels with it: one fix design ('the latch disturbs no state') covers both arms.

MEASURED, rung 3, unmodified -E cats, PIT at 0x7c000040, five controls green in every run (RAM liveness, CP15 MMU-off readback, a device signature RAM cannot produce, an MMU-ON negative control, encodings checked against the emulator's own disassembly):
    committed HEAD  mode_byte after latch 0x00 (DESTROYED), latched reads 0x00 0x00,
                    two 'huh? reading from counter 0' complaints
    shipped         mode_byte after latch 0x24 (PRESERVED), 0 complaints,
                    findcpuspeed divisor 65535 (safe)

THE DETECTOR KILLS PER VARIANT, INCLUDING THE OVER-FIX:
                    R1 clobber   R2 false error   R3 divisor
    committed HEAD     FAIL          FAIL            ok
    C1 panel shape      ok            ok            FAIL = 0
    C2 read-arm only   FAIL           ok             ok
    shipped             ok            ok             ok
R3 exists specifically to catch the plausible over-fix the panel recommended.

*** THE SEAT CAUGHT A VACUITY BUG IN ITS OWN FIRST DRAFT: *** the rows read absent registers as ok (-1 == -1), so three 'kills' were runs that never started -- an execvp PATH bug. Rows now fail on absent data (R0), and R0 is why the table above can be believed.

FOUR CLAIMS IN MY BRIEF MEASURED FALSE, and one of them I had propagated all evening: fatal() is NOT 'byte-for-byte debug()' -- debug() returns early under quiet_mode/verbosity and fatal() never does, so a fatal() flood CANNOT BE SILENCED even with -q, which makes every flood row MORE severe. The guest function is gettick(), not microtime(). d->mode[] is behaviourally inert (written in three places, read only inside a debug() printf), so pitclobber's only guest-visible effect is via mode_byte. And 'return the reload value' does not return the reload value.

*** EVIDENCE 2026-08-27: THE PREMISE IS TRUE AND THE FRAMING AS A DEFECT IS WRONG -- the limitation is DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED AND REASONED. But there is a narrow mechanical subset the stated reasoning does NOT cover, and I hit it myself today. ***

**The tool says so in its own header** (`check_witness.py:38-41`):
  > *"The check enforces the SHAPE, not the truth: it cannot tell whether `probe:foo.py` really preserves routing. **That judgement stays with the panel, which is the honest division** -- a script that claimed to validate a witness would be exactly the false comfort the ladder was written against."*

**That reasoning is correct and should not be overturned.** *Does this artefact actually witness the defect?* is a judgement about routing and controls; a script asserting it would manufacture confidence, which is the precise failure the witness ladder exists to prevent.

*** BUT THE EXEMPTION IS BROADER THAN ITS REASON. *** The reason covers a JUDGEMENT. Two adjacent facts are not judgements at all:
  * **does the named file EXIST?** -- one `os.path.isfile`;
  * **does ANY gate reference it?** -- one grep over `regress/gate_*.sh`.
**Neither claims the witness is valid. Both catch a witness that cannot possibly be valid**, and a witness naming a file no gate ever runs is in that category.

**I PRODUCED A LIVE INSTANCE TODAY.** Back-filling [[exitsweep]]'s witness I wrote that its probe was *wired into TWO gates ... so it actually runs*. It is run by ONE (`gate_m88k_rounding.sh`); the other only counts its constructs in a census. **Section K passed that field**, because the string's shape was valid. A gate-reference grep would have reddened my overclaim in the commit that made it.

rows.state_note:
*** EVIDENCE 2026-08-27: TRUE, LATENT, and now QUANTIFIED EXACTLY -- 12 of 14. The remedy is already in the same file, applied to the other 2. ***

**The shape**, `precommit_check.sh:710-718` (the witness checker, representative of all 14):
```sh
if [ ! -f "$WITCHK" ]; then
        warn "check_witness.py MISSING -- witness naming NOT verified"    # SOFT
elif out=$(python "$WITCHK" 2>&1); then  good ...
else    bad "A ROW CLOSED WITH COMMITS AND NO ADMISSIBLE WITNESS:"        # HARD
```
**A checker that FAILS is a hard failure. A checker that is ABSENT is a warning.** So deleting the file converts a hard gate into a soft one, and the commit proceeds.

**THE CENSUS (deriver: `grep -cE '\[ ! -f .*(CHK|check_)'` then the following line):**
```
  checkers guarded          14
  MISSING -> warn (soft)    12
  MISSING -> bad  (hard)     2   check_row_states.py, check_cited_artifacts.py
```

> *** THE TWO HARD ONES ARE THE FINDING. *** Somebody already decided this question for two checkers and implemented it in this exact file, so **the remedy is a transferred warrant, not a design** -- make the other twelve match the two.

**NOT guest-reachable:** it is a host-side pre-commit script; no emulated guest can delete a worktree file. **Observable:** the precommit process exit status -- 0 when broken, non-zero when fixed.

**BUT DO NOT SWEEP IT UNILATERALLY -- there is a real argument on the other side, and it is the one this project keeps citing:** a hard failure on absence means a degraded or partial checkout cannot run the gate AT ALL, and *a check that has to be switched off is worse than no check*. The counter-argument is that all fourteen live in the same repo, so absence is not a partial-checkout condition -- it is a deletion. **That is an adjudication question, not a unilateral edit**, and it changes the script every commit runs, so it also owes negative controls both ways.

*Directly relevant to today: I relied on this gate all session and it caught three real obligations. This does not undermine those catches -- a checker that RAN and failed is hard. It bounds what a green gate proves: it proves the checkers PRESENT are satisfied, not that the intended set ran.*

The shadow batc[] is what m88k_translate_v2p reads at memory_m88k.c:152 -- BEFORE the PATC and BEFORE the walk -- so a stale entry silently returns a wrong physical address for a 512 KB block. The guest programs it: pmap.c:761-772 pmap_map_batc(), live code.

Of the THREE arms in this device that touch translation inputs, two are covered and the third has zero rows. entries.note:
*** THE ORACLE DESIGN IS THE POINT: it asks the REAL m88k_translate_v2p() what an address resolves to, rather than re-implementing the BATC formula in the detector. ***  Computing the right answer in the harness and comparing it against the device's array asserts something STRICTLY WEAKER than 'the device's array is what translation reads' -- which is exactly the fixed-point-oracle shape the flagship pass named as escape family #1 this morning. Three controls rather than one, so 'the expected paddr came back' cannot be a constant.

*** FINDING 1: A MUTANT ESCAPED EVERYTHING, AND THE ROUND'S OWN HARDENING CREATED IT. ***  Widening the translator's virtual match from 0xfff80000 to 0xfff00000 survived all 45 rows and both differentials. The first port table used CONSECUTIVE LBAs (0x100..0x107), which caught that mutant BY ACCIDENT -- port n's address hit port n-1's entry. Scattering the LBAs to close a DIFFERENT hole (a masked top bit no row could see) SILENTLY REMOVED THAT ACCIDENTAL COVERAGE, and only re-running the whole census after the fixture change surfaced it.

That is a general lesson worth more than the row: A FIXTURE CHANGE CAN DELETE COVERAGE NOBODY KNEW THEY HAD, and no row goes red to say so. Closed by F17, which asserts the block boundary EXPLICITLY -- first byte in, last byte in, byte below, byte above, per port -- instead of relying on an occupied neighbour. F17 is currently the ONLY row defending that property.

FINDING 2: the seat's own chosen mutant escaped -- c-> vs cpu-> on the purge callback POINTER -- and it graded it honestly as an EQUIVALENT MUTANT and a SHAPE PIN rather than a live defect, because cpu_m88k.c:121-122 gives every m88k cpu the same function with no branch. But it checked whether that is ARCHITECTURAL and found it is not: cpu_mips.c:120-133 and cpu_ppc.c:122-135 install DIFFERENT callbacks per cpu width. Closed with a second spy and row J6.

It also SIMULATED selfmutant.py's tree shape exactly -- symlink mirror plus one real file -- to prove the new #include resolves and both row-ids still name exactly one row, WITHOUT running a gate. Build 0.74 s against a 120 s limit.

rows.witness: none, and none can exist without first changing the function: both `exit(1)` sites are unreachable by the enclosing function's own control flow (see the note). A witness would have to add a `goto exception` that skips the status assignment, which is laundering, not witnessing.
rows.state_note:
*** EVIDENCE 2026-08-27: the CALLS EXIST (claim true) but BOTH SITES ARE UNREACHABLE. This is dormant defensive code, NOT a live host kill -- a real severity downgrade, and the point of establishing it is to stop a round being opened on 'a surviving exit(1)'. ***

`src/cpus/memory_m88k.c` contains exactly **two** `exit(1)` calls, both inside the `switch (pfsr_status)` that runs after the `exception:` label:
  * `:390-394` -- `case CMMU_PFSR_SUCCESS:`, whose own diagnostic reads *"HUH? CMMU_PFSR_SUCCESS:, but exception? TODO"*;
  * `:408-413` -- `default:`, *"Internal error in memory_m88k?"*.

**Both are internal-invariant assertions, and the invariant holds structurally.** `pfsr_status` is initialised to `CMMU_PFSR_SUCCESS` at `:118`, which is what makes the first case look live. But the exception block is reached ONLY through the `exception:` label at `:373`, and:

  * there are **seven** `goto exception` sites -- `:173`, `:213`, `:267`, `:275`, `:300`, `:309`, `:341` -- and **each is preceded, ONE LINE ABOVE, by a fault assignment** at `:172`, `:212`, `:266`, `:274`, `:299`, `:308`, `:340`. Seven gotos, seven assignments, gap of 1 in every case.
  * **control cannot FALL THROUGH into the label**: `:370` is `return (accumulated_flags & PG_RO)? 1 : 2;`, immediately above it.

So `pfsr_status` is never `CMMU_PFSR_SUCCESS` at `:388`, and the `default:` arm is unreachable for the same reason -- the seven assigned values are exactly WRITE, SFAULT, SUPER and PFAULT, and all four have their own cases at `:397-406`.

**DISPOSITION: assessed, NOT a live defect, and it ranks BELOW anything guest-drivable.** The fork de-fatalises sites a guest can drive; these are sites a guest cannot reach without a code change. That is the distinction the queue ordering depends on, and the row previously read as though this were an ordinary surviving host kill.

**WHAT WOULD RE-OPEN IT, stated so the absence record is falsifiable:** any new `goto exception` that does not assign `pfsr_status` first, or any new writer of `pfsr_status`. The check is the same one run here and it is mechanical -- **the seven gotos and seven assignments must stay paired.** If that pairing is ever broken, the `SUCCESS` case becomes live and a guest-triggered fault kills the host.

*Method note: the pairing was derived by matching each `goto exception` to the nearest preceding non-SUCCESS assignment, then confirming no fall-through path into the label. Both halves are needed -- the gap check alone would miss a fall-through, and the fall-through check alone would miss an unassigned goto.*

entries.note:
*** CREATED BY THIS ROUND'S OWN FIX, AND IT CONVERTS AN INPUT CLASS FROM LOUD-AND-WRONG TO SILENT-AND-GREEN -- the exact vacuity the round existed to remove. *** MEASURED both sides.

The smnotland fix makes an out-of-src subject WORK, including regress/ -- i.e. THE DETECTOR ITSELF. Subject regress/diff_rtc_range.c, anchor = the row's own line, one digit changed in its expected value:

    ok  pristine arm green; ok mutant killed by the named row;  SELFMUTANT_OK
src/devices/dev_rtc.c -- the code the lane exists to watch -- WAS NEVER TOUCHED. Every shipped check passes: anchor unique, old != new, exact-text postcondition, binaries differ, pristine green, row id unique. The detector was simply edited to print FAIL about itself. LATENT, NOT LIVE: all 12 shipped lanes use src/ subjects (verified). But selfmutant.py:221-225 ADVERTISES the capability ('makes an out-of-src subject WORK rather than merely be refused. Nothing uses one today') -- the invitation is written down and the guardrail is not. An inert mutant and a blind detector produce identical stdout, so that check would convert every genuine SELFMUTANT_FAIL into SETUP, making the control vacuous in exactly the case it exists for.

closure.note:

entries.note:
MEASURED on the committed build/gxemul while establishing reachability for the vr41xx site:
    e105  rc=134 (SIGABRT, core dumped)      z50                   rc=0
    be300 rc=134 (SIGABRT, core dumped)      mobilepro770          rc=0

Those three lines map to exactly BE300 (:72), E105 (:102), VR3 (:223). *** THREE BAD SITES, THREE ABORTING SUBTYPES, 1:1. ***  The /* TODO: irq? */ above :114 is the author's own flag. Upstream defect, inherited: git log shows only 39748e3. Identical in est/ and SEC.

entries.note:
*** WITNESS BUILT AND REPRODUCED, 24/24, deterministic across two runs. ***  The failing call is INTERRUPT_CONNECT(devinit->interrupt_path, d->irq) at dev_ns16550.c:342, reached only via device_add() from the machine-setup switch.

RUNG 2 IS THE CEILING, NOT A SHORTCUT, and the seat argued it rather than asserting it: a rung-3 cold-debugger probe needs a CONSTRUCTED machine and construction is what aborts; rung 4 needs that plus an image, and there is no hpcmips image in _images/. The rung-1 exclusion is respected -- nothing is #included, no function called directly, no stub substituted. Strip the machine description and this measures nothing, BECAUSE THE MACHINE DESCRIPTION IS THE DEFECT'S CARRIER. That is exactly the case the ladder licenses rung 2 for.

    subtype                      rc            class           failing name
    be-300                       -6 SIGABRT    ABORT_LOOKUP    "0"
    e-105                        -6 SIGABRT    ABORT_LOOKUP    "0"
    agenda (vr3)                 -6 SIGABRT    ABORT_LOOKUP    "17"
    workpad, mobilepro770/780/800/880   0      CONSTRUCTED_OK  --

*** THE STRONGEST CONTROL IS DERIVED FROM SOURCE CALL ORDER RATHER THAN HARDCODED, and it is also the fix-design measurement: ***  BE-300 and E-105 call device_add BEFORE dev_vr41xx_init, so the process prints SIX handlers (machine[0].cpu[0].2-7, no vrip.); VR3 calls dev_vr41xx_init first, so it prints SIXTY-FOUR including vrip.*. Both predictions matched. A DISCRIMINATION control also passes: -E mvmeppc -e mvme1600 really does SIGABRT, with a different message, and classifies ABORT_OTHER -- 'the process died' is not the same claim as 'it died HERE'.

*** A BUFFERING TRAP BIT IT FIRST, and it is worth carrying: abort() does not flush stdio, so with output to a pipe the diagnostic VANISHED and be-300 produced a 43-BYTE FILE. ***  The probe now requires stdbuf -o0 -e0 and rows go red if an aborting run's diagnostic did not arrive. A probe that reads an empty file as 'no diagnostic' would have mis-attributed the defect entirely.

LINE NUMBERS RE-DERIVED AT RUN TIME rather than remembered -- and this time the brief's were RIGHT (:84, :114, :242, cases :72, :102, :223), which is worth recording given that the previous round's brief had five wrong. Two corrections: the /* TODO: irq? */ appears above TWO of them (:83, :113), not one, and VR3 has a different TODO at :237-238. VRIP_INTR_SIU = 9 at vripreg.h:284, so VR3's 8+VRIP_INTR_SIU is 17.

entries.note:
THE FIX DESIGN IS MEASURED, NOT GUESSED -- and two obvious 'fixes' are measured WRONG.

The five working hpcmips subtypes are no model: THEY ADD NO ns16550 AT ALL. The tree's idiom is at 14 sibling sites (machine_cobalt.c:73 irq=%s.cpu[%i].5, machine_evbmips.c:74, machine_arc.c:156/161, machine_sgi.c:394/400). The registered names come from dev_vr41xx.c:691-702: "%s.cpu[%i].vrip.%i", i = 0..25. Probed on a CONSTRUCTED z50 through the same device_add -> DEVINIT -> INTERRUPT_CONNECT path:
    irq=machine[0].cpu[0].vrip.9    ACCEPTED, device added, rc=0
    irq=machine[0].cpu[0].vrip.25   accepted (last registered line)
    irq=machine[0].cpu[0].vrip.26   ABORTS  <- boundary control, so acceptance is a real lookup
    irq=0 / irq=17                  abort (matches construction)
    omit irq= entirely              *** ABORTS *** -- device.c:281-282 defaults to
                                    machine[0].cpu[0], which is NOT registered on MIPS
    irq= (empty)                    *** ABORTS *** -- interrupt.c:174-179 has NO return; the
                                    'No interrupt' branch fills the template and then FALLS
                                    INTO the scan loop and aborts anyway

*** SO 'JUST DELETE THE irq=' IS NOT A FIX, MEASURED TWICE OVER. ***  The fix is irq=%s.cpu[%i].vrip.%i with machine->path, machine->bootstrap_cpu, VRIP_INTR_SIU -- AND BE-300/E-105 MUST MOVE device_add AFTER dev_vr41xx_init, which the six-versus-sixty-four handler count proves is necessary rather than tidy.

UPSTREAM, NOT THIS FORK: git log --all on machine_hpcmips.c shows exactly one commit, 39748e3 'Import GXemul 0.7.0', and git blame attributes every line of all three sites to that boundary commit.

HONEST LIMIT the seat insisted on: whether vrip.9 is the CORRECT hardware line for these UARTs is NOT measurable here -- there is no VR41xx datasheet in _scratchpad/ (the same gap as SH). VRIP_INTR_SIU is the tree's own name for the serial unit and the source's TODO is explicitly unsure. Treat the line number as a judgement and the FORM as measured.

rows.state_note:
*** EVIDENCE 2026-08-27: TRUE, but NOT guest-visible as stated -- and the answer comes with a specific warning about the WRONG fix that sits twelve lines away. ***

The fuse-ROM word-write arm stores and the byte-write arm does not. **But that asymmetry is not guest-visible on its own:** a byte-only row cannot distinguish *ignore all writes* from *byte now stores*. **A word-write control on the same location is required**, or the detector proves nothing.

*** THE WARNING IS THE VALUABLE PART: DO NOT COPY THE NVRAM `memcpy` TWELVE LINES BELOW (`:582-589`). *** It is a *just `memcpy` any `len`* idiom, and it is **WRONG for a `uint32_t fuse_rom[]` on a little-endian host** -- the array is word-typed, so a byte-wise copy lands the bytes in host order rather than the device's. The nearest-looking idiom in the same file is the wrong one.

**What IS available:** the latched-`fatal()`-then-continue idiom at `:846-856` (`intmask_lowbits_reported[]`, from `#438`), and the inverse of the byte-read's big-endian shift at `:574`. **There is no shared byte-merge helper**, so the merge must be written.

**And a constraint on the tempting alternative:** a ROM-faithful *ignore all writes* would make the two arms consistent, but it **breaks `MACHINE_SETUP`** -- so the consistent-looking fix is not free either.

rows.title: sh4bcr  A guest 4-byte store to SH4_BCR2/BCR3 terminates the host process -- rung-3 witnessed, 5/5 controls green, on an unmodified -E landisk

closure.note:
Shipped as 9de16b7. Badge A: the main loop implemented and wrote the detector.

*** WHAT SHOULD BE WEIGHED AGAINST THAT: SEVEN OF EIGHT SEATS SAID SHIP, AND THE NINE-ROW DETECTOR THEY WERE APPROVING PASSED SIX MUTANTS -- one of which puts exit(1) back on a guest-reachable path. ***  The single dissent was the one seat that COMPILED AND RAN. Four of the round's own errors were caught by runs rather than reasoning: the first fix WAS mutant M1 (D3 caught it); D4's first version ran the two sites in separate processes so the shared-latch mutant passed; the positive control PASSED and turned out to be a real hole rather than a dead pipeline (now D10); and D7b's expected constant was lifted from another probe with a different input.

entries.note:
*** THE SHARPEST WITNESS OF THE SESSION, AND IT IS FILED NOWHERE: *** no BCR2, BCR3 or 'Non-16-bit' appears in OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md, CHANGELOG.md or ledger.json.

MEASURED, stock build/gxemul, unmodified in-tree -E landisk, cold debugger, real SH-4 decode, real memory_rw, real device dispatch. No source edited, no device_add:
    L_liveness_RAM               alive=True  val=efbeadde              ok
    S_device_signature_BCR2      alive=True  val=fd3f0000              ok
    N_neg_ctrl_BCR1_32bit_store  alive=True                            ok
    A_DEFECT_BCR2_32bit_store    alive=False fatalmsg=True  HOST KILLED ok
    A2_DEFECT_BCR3_32bit_store   alive=False fatalmsg=True  HOST KILLED ok
A guest `mov.l r0,@r1` with r1 = 0xff800004 reaches dev_sh4.c:1409, prints 'Non-16-bit SH4_BCR2 access?' and calls exit(1). *** TWO GUEST INSTRUCTIONS, HOST GONE. ***  dev_sh4 is registered unconditionally by cpu_sh.c:200 over SH4_REG_BASE + 0x01000000, so the address is in range; being SH-4 P4 space it needs no MMU setup.

*** THE NEGATIVE CONTROL IS THE SHARP ONE: SH4_BCR1 at 0xff800000 has NO len check at all (:1399), so the same device, the same 4-byte width, FOUR BYTES AWAY, SURVIVES. *** The kill is the width test, not the device. Device signature: writing 0xffff to BCR2 at legal width reads back 0x3ffd = idata & 0x3ffd (:1413) -- RAM would have returned 0xffffffff.

*** AND THIS REFUTES THE hlen CENSUS'S OWN IMMUNITY CLAIM: *** it states 'SH-4 is provably immune', scoped to 8-byte accesses. SH-4 turns out to be the family where the host kill was MEASURED, using a 4-byte access, which SH-4 issues freely. The census's discriminator ('does it mention len') undercounts the class and so does its immunity argument.

FIX SHAPE is the #438 shape: keep the fatal() diagnostic, drop the exit(1), service at the register's natural width. Note the existing regress/sh_halt_probe.py covers cpu->running = 0 halts ONLY, not exit(1), so it is blind to this by construction.

entries.note:
*** FOUND THE BRIEF'S OWN PREMISE FALSE, AND IT WAS MINE. ***  The brief said BCR3 is at 0xff800006, adjacent to BCR2, 'so a 4-byte access spans BOTH registers'. sh4_bscreg.h:70 reads 0xff800050. No overlap exists and the whole Q2 dissolves.

MEASURED the dispatch rather than assuming it: memory_rw hands the WHOLE access to ONE handler -- one call, len=4, never split; the 1024-byte page split cannot fire on a 4-byte aligned access. Reachable guest lengths are 1, 2, 4 (an fmov pair is two separate 4-byte calls, so 8 never arrives). So the handler owns the byte lanes.

*** BIG-ENDIAN SH-4 IS CONSTRUCTIBLE TODAY, and the naive fix is measurably wrong on it: *** byte_order(big) with in-tree type("landisk") gives a real BE CPU, and there `idata & 0x3ffd` takes the WRONG halfword -- the guest's 16 bits land in the top half and read back as 0. SH4_BCR1 four lines above already consults cpu->byte_order.

Design shipped as recommended: service the register's own two bytes in the guest's byte order, diagnose once PER SITE, len < 2 early-out. Rejected 'ignore the write' on measurement -- these two were the only length checks in the file, and PCR/RTCSR/RTCNT/RTCOR/RFCR all accept any width and service it, so ignoring would make these the only two registers that silently swallow a write.

ALSO MEASURED AND NOT IN THIS ROUND: sh4_pcic in the SAME FILE has ELEVEN exit(1) sites with ~116 word offsets reaching its default:, and DEVICE_ACCESS(sh4) itself carries five more value-guard exit(1)s. Filed as [[sh4pcicexit]].

entries.note:
*** VERDICT: SHIP WITH CHANGES -- THE ONLY SEAT OF EIGHT THAT DID NOT SAY SHIP, AND IT WAS RIGHT. SIX MUTANTS ESCAPED THE 9-ROW DETECTOR. ***  All built, cmp-verified on disk, run:
    X  `if (partial && writeflag == MEM_READ) exit(1);`   9/9   *** THE HOST DIES AGAIN ***
    A  delete `& 0x3ffd` on BCR2's write                  9/9   reserved-bit mask gone
    G  add    `& 0x3ffd` on BCR3's write                  9/9   BCR3 silently loses bits
    B  `return 8*(len-2)` -> `return 0`                   9/9   the whole big-endian lane
    F  swap the Ignored/Servicing ternary                 9/9   diagnostic states the opposite of what happened
X is the answer to 'smallest edit': it reinstates exit(1) on a guest-reachable path -- the round's HEADLINE PROPERTY -- with every row green. Measured: one `mov.b @r1,r4` at 0xff800004 ends the process, exit status 1, output stops mid-instruction.

*** BOTH ROOT CAUSES WERE STRUCTURAL, NOT CARELESS. ***  (1) The reachable shapes are (read|write) x len(1|2|4) = SIX and the detector covered FIVE -- NO ROW DID A 1-BYTE READ. (2) Both write-value oracles were MASK-TRANSPARENT: D1 wrote 0x89ab3ffd and 0x3ffd & 0x3ffd is 0x3ffd; D8 wrote 0x89ab1234 and 0x1234 & 0x3ffd is 0x1234. A row NAMED 'masked' could not see the mask. One constant (0xc003 -> 0x0001) kills both.

IT ALSO MEASURED TWO OF MY COMMENTS FALSE. The `len < 2` guard's comment shouted that a 1-byte store is 'reachable -- measured'; the store is reachable but THIS FUNCTION IS NOT REACHED WITH IT, because report() returns 0 and the arm breaks first -- traced across all twelve report-calls. And the header comment argued against dropping a write while the code dropped one, which free-running is invisible because debug() computes v = verbose - 1 = -1 and returns.

RESIDUALS it named and I filed rather than fixed: partial READS are dropped where they could be serviced exactly ([[sh4partialread]]), and the precedent registers resolve BE lanes the OTHER way and PROMOTE a 1-byte write ([[sh4bsclane]]). It also predicted, untested, that a function-static latch would pass -- the M3 shape at device-instance granularity.
