FILED 2026-09-07.  Surfaced while verifying a claim in the grok seat's `lcabadval` pass-1 BODY (its
verdict line did not carry it) -- and **verified to be sharper than the seat stated it**, by opening
both functions.

**THE DEFECT: an ACCEPTED write to one register arms a host kill in a DIFFERENT function.**

`DEVICE_ACCESS(lca_ioc)`, `case LCA_IOC_CONF`:

    d->ioc_conf = idata;
    /*  Only bit 0 is implemented so far, the PCI bus 0 vs
        bus non-0 selection bit.  */
    if (idata & ~1) {
            fatal("TODO: Write to unimplemented bit of IOC_CONF: 0x%" PRIx64 "\n", ...);
            exit(1);
    }

**`0x1` PASSES that guard.**  `idata & ~1` is 0, so the write is accepted, stored, and the arm's own
comment describes bit 0 as the implemented selector.

`DEVICE_ACCESS(lca_pci_conf)` then consumes it:

    bus = d->ioc_conf & 1;
    if (bus == 0) {
            for (dev=0; dev<21; dev++)
                    if (tag & (0x800 << dev))
                            break;
            if (dev >= 21) {
                    /*  fatal("[ LCA: No bus 0 device? TODO ]\n");
                    exit(1);  */
                    dev = 0;
            }
    } else {
            fatal("TODO. Non-zero bus.\n");
            exit(1);
    }

So: **guest writes 1 to IOC_CONF (accepted), then performs any PCI configuration-space access, and
the host process exits.**  Two guest accesses, both to registers the model implements, neither of
them rejected.

*** WHY IT IS ITS OWN ROW AND NOT PART OF [[lcabadval]]. ***  Every kill `lcabadval` covers is a
guard REFUSING a value it does not recognise.  **This one fires on a value the guard ACCEPTS**, in a
different function, on a later access.  The acceptance and the kill are separated in both code and
time, which is why a per-arm audit of `lca_ioc` walks straight past it -- as mine did, twice.

*** AND THE SEAT'S FRAMING NEEDED CORRECTING, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH RECORDING. ***  grok wrote
that this exit becomes *"newly reachable from a CONF extra-bit write that also sets bit 0; today
that write dies in the CONF guard first."*  That is true of an EXTRA-BIT write (e.g. `0x3`), and it
made the kill sound like a CONSEQUENCE of adopting option A.  **It is not: `0x1` alone reaches it
today, with no fix applied.**  A widens which CONF values arrive here; it does not open the door.
The door is open now.  *Checked by reading both arms rather than by accepting the seat's sentence --
which is this project's own rule, and the seat was right about the site while being wrong about the
timing.*

**THE IRONY, and it is a design signal rather than a joke:** the `bus == 0` branch is the file's own
graceful-degradation PRECEDENT -- a commented-out `fatal()`/`exit(1)` with `dev = 0;` substituted --
and [[lcabadval]] cites that very loop as a transferable in-tree warrant.  **The `else` five lines
below it is a bare kill.**  Same function, opposite dispositions, no comment explaining why.

**REACHABILITY, stated honestly rather than assumed.**  Bit 0 is a bus SELECTOR, so a guest reaches
this by selecting a bus the model does not implement and then doing config access -- plausible for
firmware or an OS that probes beyond bus 0, and trivially reachable by a probe.  **Whether any
shipped guest on `alphabook1` actually does it is NOT established here**, and the row does not claim
it.  What is established is that no guard stands between an accepted write and the kill.

**WITNESS: a rung-3 probe is available and most of it already exists.**  `device_add(machine, "lca")`
is `ST_ALPHABOOK1` ONLY (`machine_alpha.c`), and `regress/lca_confwidth_probe.py` ALREADY drives a
guest `stq`/`ldq` at `LCA_IOC_CONF` (`0xfffffc0180000020`, K0SEG | physical) on unmodified
`alphabook1`.  This row needs one more session: `stq 0x1` to CONF, then a PCI config-space access.
**Three traps that probe already paid for:** debugger `dump` skips `DM_DEFAULT` handlers; a debugger
`put d` of a killing value IS a host kill but is NOT a guest instruction, so it does not witness; and
HAE at window offset 0 silently succeeds, so a miss control must not use `LCA_IOC_BASE+0`.

**DISPOSITION, not yet adjudicated:** it is the same de-fatalisation family, but the option set
differs because the kill is not a value refusal -- the honest members here are DECLINE THE CONFIG
ACCESS (return without dispatching, with a latched announce) or IMPLEMENT bus != 0.  **Note the
architecturally correct error path is blocked for the same reason grok gave on the sibling row:
`LCA_IOC_STAT0`/`STAT1` have no case at all and hit the `default:` arm's `exit(1)`, so LCA cannot
report a device error through the register the header designates for it.**

sev HIGH: a guest-drivable host kill, reached by two ordinary accesses with no rejected value
anywhere on the path.

*** SIBLING CHECK DISCHARGED WITH A DENOMINATOR, 2026-09-07 -- the class has EXACTLY ONE member in
this file. ***  The rule is grep for the siblings before calling a finding whole; here the question
is which lca_ioc fields have a consumer at all, since a field nothing reads cannot arm a delayed
kill.  Counting references that are neither the readback (`odata = d->X`) nor the store (`d->X = `):

    ioc_conf          1 consumer   <- `bus = d->ioc_conf & 1` in lca_pci_conf.  THIS ROW.
    tlb_enable        0
    window_base_0     0            window_base_1     0
    window_mask_0     0            window_mask_1     0
    window_t_base_0   0            window_t_base_1   0

**So the accepted-write-arms-a-later-kill shape cannot recur elsewhere in dev_lca.c**: the other
seven fields are write-and-read-back with nothing downstream.  That is also why [[lcabadval]]s five
pure-storage arms are a different problem from this one, and why a fix here does not generalise to
them.

*Not claimed beyond this file.  The general class -- an ACCEPTED store that a later access consumes
into a terminating path -- is a plausible cross-device census and is NOT run here.*

*** THE WITNESS DESIGN IS SOUND -- grok, 2026-09-07, ON THE BRIEF codex REFUSED.  The
alternate-transport rule paid off completely: the recovery is BETTER than the refused seat would

**DENOMINATOR, and it is the largest this row has seen:** all of `dev_lca.c` (390 lines -- both
handlers, `DEVINIT`, ISA, interrupt stubs); `DEVICE_ACCESS(lca_pci_conf)` and
`DEVICE_ACCESS(lca_ioc)` end to end; `bus_pci_data_access`/`bus_pci_setaddr` in `bus_pci.c`;
`alpha_translate_v2p` K0SEG in `memory_alpha.c`; the device and unmapped paths in `memory_rw.c`;
`LS_GENERIC_N`/`LS_N` in `cpu_alpha_instr_loadstore.c`; `fatal()` in `debugmsg.c`; `ST_ALPHABOOK1`
in `machine_alpha.c`; and all of `regress/lca_confwidth_probe.py`.

**CONFIRMED:** S2 reaches `bus = d->ioc_conf & 1` for ANY access in the window -- no `switch` on
`relative_addr`, no `len` test, no `writeflag` test that can skip it, no early `return`; the only
`writeflag` use before it is filling `idata`, which is not a guard.  `len` is first used AFTER the
kill.  And `ioc_conf` has **exactly two readers**, so nothing else can be armed by S1.

*** FOUR CORRECTIONS THAT CHANGE THE CONSTRUCTION: ***

1. **MY LIVENESS CONTROL IS MISLABELLED.**  `ioc rt` proves the WRITER (`lca_ioc`'s CONF arm)
   round-trips `0x1`.  **It says nothing about S2's window.**  PCI_CONF liveness is the armed
   session's unique message (the handler ran) PLUS the control surviving (the same access is not an
   unconditional kill).  A positive signature is available if wanted: an empty-slot read returns
   `0xffffffffffffffff`, where unmapped returns 0.
2. **S2 MUST BE A READ, NOT A WRITE.**  Both reach the kill, but an empty-slot WRITE makes
   `bus_pci_data_access` print `[ ... write to non-existant device ... ]` -- so the CONTROL would
   carry a second `fatal()` on stderr.  An empty-slot READ of reg 0 is the architectural ID probe
   and is silent.
3. **A TIGHTER VARIANT: ONE PROCESS, not two sessions.**  control `ldq` (survives), then S1, then
   the armed `ldq` (dies) -- **only `ioc_conf` changes between the two loads.**  Separate sessions
   are still adequate, but this removes the residual that two processes could differ in something
   that ran before the debugger prompt.
4. **KEEP IT ON `step`.**  `continue` would make the `lca_interrupt_assert`/`_deassert` stubs a
   confounder -- and `cpu_dyntrans.c` skips interrupt delivery while single-stepping anyway.

*** THE CONTRACT LIMIT, AND IT IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LINE FOR THE FIX ROUND: THIS IS A WITNESS OF
THE `exit(1)`, NOT A DETECTOR OF THE REPAIR. ***  grok: *"'Host survives, session completes' greens
for a silent `return 1` that skips `bus_pci_*` and `memory_writemax64`, for a latched announce, AND
for falling through into existing `bus_pci` with `cur_bus=1` (empty type-1 also survives)."*  So the
post-fix oracle cannot discriminate between fix members, and a round that ships one must build a row
that can.  **Post-fix caution in the same breath: if someone later implements type-1 by falling
through to `bus_pci_setaddr(bus=1, ...)`, empty bus 1 is a non-killing miss today, so the witness
goes green -- do NOT read that green as "type-1 is modelled."**

**WHY OFFSET 0 IS THE RIGHT CONTROL ADDRESS, which I had asserted without warrant:** it is not
HAE-like (HAE is an exact-address `break` in `lca_ioc`; `lca_pci_conf` has no per-offset special
case).  On the ARMED session the offset is irrelevant -- `bus == 1` exits before `tag`/`dev` are
used.  On the SURVIVING control, `tag == 0` matches no IDSEL bit, so the `dev >= 21` body runs --
**and that body is already the commented-out kill with `dev = 0;`** -- then an empty-slot read
returns `(uint64_t)-1` without exiting.  `0x18` (the NetBSD `| 0x3 << 3` encoding) yields the same
`tag`/`reg` and is equivalent.  **Do NOT use `relative_addr = 0x800000`**, which talks to the
registered `i82378zb` at device 7.

*** AND grok FOUND THE DESIGN ARGUMENT SITTING FIVE LINES ABOVE THE DEFECT: the `dev >= 21` arm is
ALREADY DE-FATALISED, in the same function, and the surviving control USES that path. ***  *"If that
`exit(1)` were still live, the control would die and you would misread PCI_CONF as unconditionally
fatal.  The file already contains the decline precedent the `else` lacks."*  That is the strongest
available warrant for declining here, and it is one function away from the kill.

Also confirmed: FAULT (member 5) is unavailable -- `memory_rw.c` delivers a failed device access as
an exception only under `MEM_MIPS`/`MEM_M88K`, and this path always `return 1` on the live path, so
the kill is `exit(1)` and not `return 0`.  And `lca_isa`'s `ofs > len` kill is a DIFFERENT window
(`LCA_PCI_SIO`), not reachable from `0x1e0000000`.

*** CROSS-REFERENCE, AND A CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN NOVELTY CLAIM.  [[lcabadval]] ALREADY
ENUMERATED THIS KILL ON 2026-09-06. ***

Its eleven-kill census for dev_lca.c lists **line 134, class BUS, condition `bus != 0`, i.e.
`d->ioc_conf & 1`** -- so the site AND its dependence on ioc_conf were both already recorded, and I
filed this row saying only lcabadval mentioned lca_pci_conf without reading how.  **Sixth
rediscovery this session; see [[refilingclass]], which predicts exactly this.**

**WHAT THIS ROW GENUINELY ADDS, stated narrowly:** the census records the MECHANISM; it does not
record that **`0x1` PASSES the CONF guard**.  That is what makes the kill reachable with no rejected
value anywhere on the path -- an accepted write in one handler arming a terminating branch in
another -- and it is why the disposition differs from lcabadval's six value guards, whose kills all
fire on refusal.  Plus the witness design, now reviewed SOUND by grok.

**KEPT AS A SEPARATE ROW** because it has its own disposition (decline the config access, or
implement bus != 0) and its own witness, and because folding it into a row named for VALUE GUARDS
would hide it -- which is the census's own closing lesson: *a row named after one class hides the
members of the others.*

*** AND THE CENSUS NAMES SOMETHING PLAUSIBLY WORSE THAN THIS ROW, WHICH I SHOULD SAY OUT LOUD RATHER
THAN LEAVE IN A TABLE: the two INTERRUPT STUBS at :73 and :85. ***  `lca_interrupt_assert` and
`lca_interrupt_deassert` are bare `fatal("...TODO"); exit(1)` with **NO GUARD AT ALL**, so *any*
device asserting an interrupt through the LCA ends the process regardless of what it writes.  In the
census's words: the value-guard registers *"need a firmware revision that writes something else;
these two need only that an interrupt is asserted."*  That is member 7 (IMPLEMENT) of the option
set -- a whole path stubbed out, with no value being refused -- and it is a stronger candidate for
the next critical round than this one.

*** THE RUNG-3 WITNESS EXISTS AND THE DEFECT IS MEASURED, 2026-09-07.  regress/lca_confbus_probe.py,
artifact regress/artifacts/lcaconfbus1kill/witness_HEAD_20260907.raw, sentinel LCACONFBUS_DONE. ***

    bus ctl      yes                    yes                    CONTROL: identical read at ioc_conf==0 survived   ok
    bus ctlsig   0xffffffffffffffff     0xffffffffffffffff     DEVICE SIGNATURE: empty-slot ID probe             ok
    bus kill     dead                   alive                  <- THE DEFECT                                     FAIL
    bus attrib   yes                    yes                    death carried THIS arm@s diagnostic               ok
      EVIDENCE: TODO. Non-zero bus.
    LCACONFBUS_RESULT=3/4

**One emulator process, unmodified `alphabook1`, real guest instructions through real address
decode.**  The sequence is: guest `ldq` from `LCA_PCI_CONF+0` with `ioc_conf == 0` (SURVIVES), then
guest `stq 0x1` to `LCA_IOC_CONF` (ACCEPTED -- `idata & ~1` is 0), then the IDENTICAL `ldq` again
(HOST DIES).  Only `ioc_conf` differs between the two loads, which is what attributes the death to
the VALUE rather than to the address, the width, or touching the window at all.

*** grok@s PREDICTED DEVICE SIGNATURE CAME BACK EXACTLY. ***  It reasoned from `bus_pci.c` that an
empty-slot read returns `0xffffffffffffffff` via `memory_writemax64` while UNMAPPED returns 0.  The
control row reads **0xffffffffffffffff**.  That is a prediction from source, confirmed by
measurement -- so the signature control is established, not assumed.

**ORACLE POLARITY is the ladder@s: the rows assert the CORRECT (post-fix) behaviour, so `bus kill`
is RED on the committed build and goes GREEN when the defect is fixed, with the SAME script.**
Clause (i) is therefore HALF discharged -- the pre-fix symptom is shown; the post-fix green awaits a
fix, which is correct for test-first.

*** TWO APPARATUS DEFECTS CAUGHT IN THE FIRST RUN AND FIXED, both worth keeping. ***
1. **The first artifact carried NO EVIDENCE for `bus attrib`.**  The row tested the PTY buffer and
   printed nothing, so the preserved log showed a green row whose diagnostic a later reader could
   not check.  The probe now ECHOES the matched line into its own output.  *A green row whose
   evidence is not in the artifact is not verifiable, however sound the logic.*
2. **I nearly filed a false correction to grok.**  It said the `TODO. Non-zero bus.` literal is
   unique in `src/`; my grep returned TWO.  The second hit is `dev_lca.o`, the compiled object.  One
   source site, `dev_lca.c:133`.  grok was right; my apparatus swept binaries.

*** THE FIX DESIGN IS CLEARER THAN THIS ROW ASSUMED, AND IT DIVERGES FROM ITS SIBLING FOR A REASON
WORTH STATING.  Derived 2026-09-07 from the codex fix design on [[lcairqstubkill]] plus this row's
own witness. ***

**THE TWO LCA ROWS LOOK LIKE ONE PROBLEM AND ARE NOT.**  Both are bare `fatal()+exit(1)` reached by
ordinary guest access, so it is tempting to give them one disposition.  The difference is what the
guest is ASKING FOR:

* [[lcairqstubkill]] -- an interrupt DELIVERY.  There is no correct answer that is not delivery: a
  decline LOSES AN EVENT, silently or otherwise, and the guest can never learn of it.  codex's
  disposition there is "diagnose and stop the guest CPU", because continuing is a lie.
* **THIS ROW -- a PCI configuration cycle on bus 1.  There IS a correct answer, and hardware gives
  it: a config read of an absent device returns ALL ONES.**  An unimplemented BUS is legitimately
  EMPTY.  Declining is not a lost event; it is the architecturally right reply.

> **So the dispositions properly differ, and the reason is not "one is worse".  For a DELIVERY path
> an unimplemented target has no honest continuation; for an ADDRESSING path it has one, and the
> tree already implements it.**

*** AND THE TREE ALREADY DOES THE RIGHT THING ONE STEP DOWN, which the witness measured by accident.
***  The `bus == 0` branch already reaches `bus_pci_setaddr` / `bus_pci_data_access`, and this row's
own witness recorded the result: **a read of an empty slot returns `0xffffffffffffffff`** (the
`bus ctlsig` row, MEASURED).  grok noted the same about the armed side in its design review --
*"falling through into existing bus_pci with cur_bus=1 (empty type-1 also survives)"*.

**SO THE LIKELY FIX IS NOT A DECLINE AT ALL BUT A FALL-THROUGH:** stop special-casing `bus != 0`,
let the existing `bus_pci` path handle it, and an empty bus 1 answers all-ones by itself.  That is
option-set member 7 (IMPLEMENT) reached cheaply, because the machinery exists -- unlike the sibling

**WHY grok's IS WORSE, and why `M12_regnull` does not cover it.**  `M12` nulls the ternary's
else-VALUE: a non-zero register still takes the refusal arm and merely gets the wrong answer.

Its closing prescription: *"If M10_regconj comes back 14/14, the row it wants is a type-1 access at
0:7:0 **register 4**, both directions, with the same anti-wants as `t1 dev7rd` / `t1 dev7wr` (real
config data / `device 7, function 0 (i82378zb)`).  **A value-0 row at an empty slot will not do.**"*

**`t1 reg4` IS at 0:7:0 register 4** -- `T1_D7R4 = LCA_PCI_CONF + 0x070080 + BYTE_ENABLES`, re-derived
as tag 0x3800 -> bus 0, dev 7, func 0, reg 0x04.  So the address half of the prescription was already
met, and grok's warning about an empty slot is exactly why the pre-table block had deferred a bare
`reg != 0` row in the first place.

**RESIDUAL 1 -- ONE DIRECTION, NOT BOTH.**  I built the READ at reg 4 and not the WRITE.  The read
alone kills `M13_regconj` (the forward returns the device's `0x00000003` against a want of `0x0`), so
the mutant in hand is covered; what is NOT covered is a variant that spares reads at non-zero
registers and forwards only writes.  **DISCLOSED, not built.**

**RESIDUAL 2 -- THE BUS AXIS, and grok named it while explicitly declining to propose it:**

> *"Not proposing: `bus = 1` in the type-1 branch (collapses every non-zero bus onto the one
> `t1 anchor` samples).  That also sweeps, and it is the original cycle-type/bus conflation without
> the `exit(1)`.  It does not hit 0:7:0 -- those tags get bus 1, which is empty -- so it is a decode
> collapse, not a reopening of the misrouting.  **A later bus-2 tuple row would catch it; this one
> does not need that row to be a defect.**"*

**That is a FOURTH frozen axis** -- every type-1 row uses bus 0 or bus 1, so hardcoding `bus = 1`
sweeps.  It is a real defect and a LESSER one: it collapses the decode without reaching the populated
slot.  **A single bus-2 tuple row closes it.**

detector has already grown 4 -> 18 rows inside one round, three of those additions from this single
ask.  Clause (e) exists precisely for this: **a contract that names what it does not cover is
falsifiable; one that claims completeness is not.**  grok's own framing supports stopping -- *"this
one does not need that row to be a defect"* -- and the probe header will carry both residuals by
name, so a later escape is *"outside the contract, as stated"* rather than an argument about
overclaiming.

**The round therefore ships an 18-row detector with TWO NAMED HOLES: the write direction at a
non-zero register, and any bus value other than 0 or 1.**

(1) THE CHANNEL LINE.  The PRE-TABLE block's CHANNEL check says a row's channel-under-its-mutant is knowable at WRITING time, and the carrier asked the first mandated application to CHECK that claim rather than obey it.  MEASURED SCORE: 1 FOUND, 2 MISSED -- and all three were ONE mistake, which is why I think it is a rule question and not three slips.  I named each channel by asking what the code prints on the path I HAD IN MIND, never what it prints on the path THE MUTANT takes. (a) I claimed row `t1 alias' kills a writeflag-conditioned mutant.  In the MIRROR polarity it does not, and the grok seat MEASURED that the mutant sweeps an 11-row probe clean -- because every alias row used dev 0, an EMPTY slot, where forwarding returns the same all-ones the refusal synthesises.  (b) Row `t1 dev7wr', the row ADDED to close (a), matched the EMPTY-SLOT diagnostic at 0:7:0 -- the one address in this device where the slot is NOT empty.  Its channel could not fire under any mutant, ever.  The kill table's evidence echo caught it while the row itself scored GREEN under the mutant it was written for.  PROPOSED SECOND HALF OF THE RULE: name the observable, then TRACE THE MUTANT'S OWN CONTROL FLOW to the statement that emits it -- a channel is established only when you can point at the exact print reached UNDER THE MUTANT, not under the fix.  IS THAT WORTH ADDING TO THE MANDATED BLOCK?  THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT I CANNOT SETTLE MYSELF: all three misses WERE caught -- two by seats, one by the table -- so the existing machinery worked, and the amendment may be buying a check the panel and the ask-again already perform, at the cost of making an already-heavy pre-table block heavier.  (2) AN UNADJUDICATED DISAGREEMENT ON THE DISPOSITION.  deepseek: the refusal needs no announce, since a type-1 probe of bus 0 is legitimate and silence matches the empty-slot read contract.  The kimi substitute: a house `(once)' latched announce on the DISCARDED WRITE ONLY is better -- reads are legitimate probing, but a WRITE to a structurally-invalid target is almost always a driver bug, and a once-announce there costs nothing and restores the debuggability the deleted fatal() provided.  I HAVE SHIPPED SILENCE, on the ground that this file's own de-fatalised sibling (the `dev >= 21' scan-miss arm) substitutes a value and announces nothing, so silence is the in-file idiom.  Which is right?  Note the seats split along a real line rather than a vague one: both agree reads should be silent, and disagree only about the write.

FILED 2026-09-07.  **NOT a new discovery of the SITE** -- [[lcabadval]]'s eleven-kill census already
enumerated `:73` and `:85` and called them *"plausibly the most severe of the eleven"*.  What was
missing is a ROW: the census names them inside a row titled for VALUE GUARDS, which is the census's
own closing lesson (*a row named after one class hides the members of the others*), and
`OUTSTANDING_BUGS.md` mentioned them **zero** times.

**THE SITE, verbatim -- there is no predicate at all:**

    void lca_interrupt_assert(struct interrupt *interrupt)
    {
            fatal("lca_interrupt_assert: TODO\n");
            exit(1);
    }

    void lca_interrupt_deassert(struct interrupt *interrupt)
    {
            fatal("lca_interrupt_deassert: TODO\n");
            exit(1);
    }

*** THE WIRING, DERIVED BY READING `DEVINIT(lca)` -- AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS SEVERE. ***

    memset(&interrupt_template, 0, sizeof(interrupt_template));
    interrupt_template.line = 0;
    interrupt_template.name = interrupt_path;                        /*  "<machine>.lca"  */
    interrupt_template.extra = d;
    interrupt_template.interrupt_assert   = lca_interrupt_assert;
    interrupt_template.interrupt_deassert = lca_interrupt_deassert;
    interrupt_handler_register(&interrupt_template);

    bus_isa_init(devinit->machine, interrupt_path,
        BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1, LCA_ISA_BASE, LCA_ISA_MEMBASE);

**The stubs are registered as the handlers for `<machine>.lca`, and `bus_isa_init` is handed THAT
SAME PATH together with `BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1`.**  So the ISA bus -- both IDE controllers
included -- routes its interrupts into a function whose entire body is `fatal()` + `exit(1)`.  The
file's own comment above the stub says *"Line 0 = ISA interrupt."*

**WHY IT IS PLAUSIBLY THE WORST KILL IN THE FILE.**  Every other terminating call in `dev_lca.c`
needs a guest to write a value the model does not expect.  **This one needs only that an interrupt
is asserted** -- i.e. ordinary disk activity on a machine whose DEVINIT attaches two IDE channels.
No unusual value, no undocumented register, no firmware revision.

*** WHAT IS ESTABLISHED AND WHAT IS NOT -- read this before quoting the row. ***
* **ESTABLISHED, by reading:** the stubs terminate unconditionally; they are registered as the
  interrupt handlers; `bus_isa_init` receives the same interrupt path with both IDE channels.
* **NOT ESTABLISHED:** that any guest actually reaches them.  **No measurement has been made.**  A
  device could conceivably never assert on this path, and `interrupt_handler_register` semantics
  have not been read here.  The row does NOT claim "alphabook1 cannot boot"; it claims the wiring
  is present and the handler is a kill.

**NEXT STEP IS A RUNG-3 ATTEMPT, and the apparatus already exists.**
`regress/lca_confbus_probe.py` (shipped 2026-09-07 for [[lcaconfbus1kill]]) already boots
unmodified `alphabook1` under the debugger with a disk image attached and drives guest `ldq`/`stq`
through real decode.  The question is whether a guest access can make an IDE channel assert while
single-stepping -- **and the carrier's rule cuts against it: a step-based probe sees a SYNCHRONOUS
assert (a device handler reached inside the guest's own store) but NOT one that depends on a
host-timer callback.**  So the honest first question is *what produces the assert*, and if the
answer is `timer_add`, this needs a free-running probe rather than a stepped one.

**DISPOSITION: option-set MEMBER 7 (IMPLEMENT), and the set's other members do not apply.**  There
is no value being refused and nothing to decline, accept, mask or fault -- it is an entire path
stubbed out.  The carrier added member 7 on 2026-09-06 from this very file, using these very
functions as its example.  A cheaper interim is member 3 (decline + LATCHED announce): return
without asserting, announce once, and let the guest see a missing interrupt rather than a dead host
-- **but that trades a host kill for a silently lost interrupt**, which is the readback-lie shape
[[lcabadval]] is currently held on, so it is a design question and not an obvious win.

**TRANSFERABLE PRECEDENT, already closed in this tree:** [[lunaabsentcpu]] -- *"dev_luna88k.c
reassert_interrupts() calls the NULL interrupt callback of an UNCONFIGURED cpu slot"* -- same family
(a terminating/absent interrupt callback reached by ordinary operation), fixed, and closed with a
rung-3 probe witness (`regress/luna_absentcpu_probe.py`).  Read that round before designing this one.

sev HIGH on the wiring; it would be CRITICAL if a witness lands, and the row says so rather than
pre-judging it.

*** THE WITNESS-SHAPE QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND FAVOURABLY: THE ASSERT IS GUEST-DRIVEN, NOT
HOST-TIMER-DRIVEN, SO A STEPPED PROBE CAN REACH IT. ***

The carrier demands one question before designing any probe around a tick: *what produces the thing
the tick consumes?*  If the answer is `timer_add`, the probe must free-run, because `debugger.c`
calls `timer_stop()` while interacting and `step N` returns before `timer_start()`.

    DEVICE_TICK(wdc)
    {
            struct wdc_data *d = (struct wdc_data *) extra;

            if (d->int_assert)
                    INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq);
    }

**What it consumes is `d->int_assert`, a flag the COMMAND PATH sets from an ordinary guest register
write.**  No host timer produces it.  And tick functions do run while stepping -- `machine.c`
decrements `ticks_till_next[te]` by 1 under `single_step` instead of by `N_SAFE_DYNTRANS_LIMIT` --
so the tick fires, one tick at a time.

> **PREDICTED ROUTE: a guest write issues a wdc command that sets `int_assert`; the probe steps far
> enough for the tick to run; `INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq)` dispatches to the registered handler for
> `<machine>.lca`; and that handler is `fatal()` + `exit(1)`.**  Synchronous in the carrier's sense
> -- what the tick consumes comes from the guest, not from SIGALRM.

**STILL A PREDICTION, AND THREE LINKS ARE UNVERIFIED:** (1) that `INTERRUPT_ASSERT` on `d->irq`
resolves to the LCA handler rather than to an intermediate ISA controller that swallows it; (2) how
many steps the tick needs; (3) whether `alphabook1` reaches a state where a wdc command can be
issued from a cold debugger at all.

**LINK (1) IS THE ONE TO READ FIRST.**  `bus_isa_init` may interpose its own interrupt controller
between the IDE channel and the `<machine>.lca` path -- in which case the assert never reaches these
stubs, and the row's severity drops sharply.  **If it interposes, THAT is the finding, not a
failure**, and the row should be re-graded rather than quietly dropped.

*Recorded because it converts an open-ended witness question into three named, checkable links.*

*** A PROCESS NOTE, because it happened while writing THIS paragraph and it is the second instance
today. ***  The first attempt to record the above went through `python -c '...'` and bash tore the
single-quoted string apart on the apostrophes in "guest's" and "carrier's", exactly as it had done
hours earlier on a different note.  **The rule minted from the first instance -- PROSE DESTINED FOR
A RECORD GOES INTO A SCRIPT FILE, NEVER THROUGH `-c` -- was already written down in this same ledger
when I broke it again.**  That is the carrier's own structure-versus-memory finding landing on me
twice in one session: knowing a rule and having it fire on the right object are different problems,
and only the second is solved by writing more.  This paragraph was written from a file and landed
intact on the first attempt.

*** LINK (1) IS SETTLED BY READING, AND IT RAISES THE SEVERITY RATHER THAN LOWERING IT.  THE
INTERPOSED PIC DOES NOT SWALLOW THE ASSERT -- IT FORWARDS IT, AND BOTH STUBS ARE REACHABLE. ***

I flagged `bus_isa_init` as possibly interposing a controller that absorbs the interrupt.  **It does
interpose, and it forwards.**  The full chain, every link read:

    dev_wdc.c    DEVICE_TICK(wdc):  if (d->int_assert) INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq);
                                    -- d->irq is "<machine>.lca.isa.14" (wdc0_irq = 14,
                                       wdc1_irq = 15, bus_isa.c:180)

    bus_isa.c    isa_interrupt_assert():  sets the PIC IRR bit for that line, then
                                          isa_interrupt_common(d, old_isa_assert)

    bus_isa.c    isa_interrupt_common():  cascades PIC2 -> PIC1 IRQ 2, then
                                          new_isa_assert = d->pic1->irr & ~d->pic1->ier;
                                          if (old == new) return;
                                          if (!new) { INTERRUPT_DEASSERT(d->irq); return; }
                                          ... otherwise asserts upward

    dev_lca.c    lca_interrupt_assert() / lca_interrupt_deassert():
                                          fatal("...TODO"); exit(1);

**`d->irq` in `bus_isa_data` is the connection made at `bus_isa.c:193`:
`INTERRUPT_CONNECT(interrupt_base_path, d->irq)` -- and `DEVINIT(lca)` passes `interrupt_path` =
`"<machine>.lca"` as that base path.  So the upward assert lands exactly on the two stubs.**

**AND `BUS_ISA_EXTERNAL_PIC` IS NOT SET BY LCA**, so the whole block at `bus_isa.c:190-209` runs:
LCA passes only `BUS_ISA_IDE0 | BUS_ISA_IDE1`.  The 16 ISA lines are registered and the upward
connection is made.

*** BOTH DIRECTIONS KILL, WHICH I HAD NOT EXPECTED. ***  `isa_interrupt_common` calls
**`INTERRUPT_DEASSERT(d->irq)`** at the point where the last unmasked IRR bit clears -- and
`lca_interrupt_deassert` is the same bare `fatal()` + `exit(1)`.  So an ordinary interrupt LIFECYCLE
-- assert, then acknowledge -- reaches a terminating stub at BOTH ends.  A fix that de-fatalises
only the assert leaves the deassert live.

**THE ONE REMAINING GATE, and it is NOT a guest-unmask requirement in the direction I first
assumed:** the upward assert fires when `pic1->irr & ~pic1->ier` becomes non-zero, i.e. when an IRR
bit is set and NOT masked by `ier`.  **`ier` is the PIC's interrupt-ENABLE/mask register, and its
RESET VALUE has NOT been read here** (`dev_8259.c`).  If it starts at 0 -- nothing masked -- then
the FIRST IDE assert propagates immediately with no guest setup at all.  **That is the next thing to
read, and it decides whether this is "reachable after ordinary driver setup" or "reachable
immediately".**  Recorded as unread rather than guessed.

**SEVERITY STAYS HIGH AND IS NOT RAISED TO CRITICAL YET**, because reachability is still established
by READING only -- no witness has been run.  What has changed is that the plausible-interposition
escape hatch is now closed: the PIC forwards, and both stubs are on the path.

*** THE LAST GATE IS OPEN AT RESET.  THE CHAIN IS NOW COMPLETE WITH EVERY LINK READ, AND IT NEEDS NO
GUEST SETUP AT ALL. ***

The remaining question was the PIC mask: the upward assert fires when `pic1->irr & ~pic1->ier` goes
non-zero, so a non-zero reset `ier` would mask IDE and gate the whole path behind guest driver
configuration.  Read:

    dev_8259.c:266    memset(d, 0, sizeof(struct pic8259_data));
    dev_8259.c:213    d->ier = idata;          <- the ONLY write to ier, from a guest store

**`ier` is zeroed at init and is never set anywhere else.**  So at reset `ier == 0`, `irr & ~ier`
is just `irr`, and **the FIRST set IRR bit propagates upward immediately.**  Nothing is masked until
a guest deliberately masks it.

*** THE COMPLETE CHAIN, EVERY LINK READ IN THE SOURCE: ***

    1.  dev_wdc.c      DEVICE_TICK(wdc): if (d->int_assert) INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq);
                       `int_assert` is set by the guest COMMAND path -- no host timer involved.
                       d->irq is "<machine>.lca.isa.14"  (wdc0_irq = 14, wdc1_irq = 15)

    2.  bus_isa.c      isa_interrupt_assert(): sets the PIC IRR bit, calls isa_interrupt_common()

    3.  bus_isa.c      isa_interrupt_common(): new = pic1->irr & ~pic1->ier;  ier == 0 AT RESET,
                       so `new` is non-zero on the first assert -> forwards upward on d->irq
                       (and calls INTERRUPT_DEASSERT(d->irq) when the last unmasked bit clears)

    4.  bus_isa.c:193  d->irq came from INTERRUPT_CONNECT(interrupt_base_path, d->irq), and
                       DEVINIT(lca) passes interrupt_path = "<machine>.lca" as that base path

    5.  dev_lca.c:70   lca_interrupt_assert():   fatal("...TODO"); exit(1);
        dev_lca.c:82   lca_interrupt_deassert(): fatal("...TODO"); exit(1);

**So on `alphabook1`, an ordinary IDE interrupt ends the host process, and BOTH ends of the
interrupt lifecycle -- assert and deassert -- land on a terminating stub.**  No unusual register
value, no undocumented offset, no firmware revision, and no guest PIC configuration: the mask is
open at reset.

*** WHAT IS AND IS NOT CLAIMED, because this is the point at which overclaiming would be easy. ***
* **ESTABLISHED BY READING, link by link:** the wiring, the forwarding, the open reset mask, and
  that both stubs terminate unconditionally.
* **NOT MEASURED.**  No probe has been run.  Nothing here shows that a guest on `alphabook1`
  actually issues a wdc command that sets `int_assert`, nor that the tick runs before the guest
  does something else.  **The row does NOT claim "alphabook1 cannot boot"** -- that is a plausible
  consequence, not a finding, and it would need a witness.
* The severity assessment therefore stays **HIGH on the wiring**.  It goes to the top of the
  critical queue only when a witness lands, and the honest form of that sentence is what this row
  says rather than what it implies.

**A FIX MUST TAKE BOTH STUBS.**  De-fatalising only `lca_interrupt_assert` leaves
`lca_interrupt_deassert` live on the same path, reached at acknowledge time -- which would convert
"dies on the first disk interrupt" into "dies on the first disk interrupt ACK" and read as a fix in
every test that only asserts.

*Found by following [[lcabadval]]'s own eleven-kill census, which had already named these two as
"plausibly the most severe of the eleven" and which nothing had followed up.*

*** CORRECTION TO THIS ROW'S OWN PRECEDENT CLAIM: [[lunaabsentcpu]] TRANSFERS AS A **WITNESS**
TECHNIQUE AND **NOT** AS A DISPOSITION.  Checked by reading its diff rather than its title. ***

The row above says *"read that round before designing this one"*, which reads as though its FIX
transfers.  It does not.  `79cd12e`'s diff on `dev_luna88k.c` is a **BOUND** repair:

    -   for (cpu = 0; cpu < MAX_CPUS; cpu++)
    +   for (cpu = 0; cpu < d->ncpus; cpu++)          /*  #503  */

plus a captured `ncpus` snapshot.  **luna's defect was walking into UNPOPULATED slots and calling a
callback that was the memset's NULL** -- a SIGSEGV from an absent handler.  **LCA's defect is a
handler that is PRESENT and deliberately terminates.**  Bounding a walk cannot help when the walk is
correct and the destination is `exit(1)`; there is no unconnected slot here.

**WHAT DOES TRANSFER, and it is the more useful half: HOW TO DRIVE AN INTERRUPT FROM GUEST STORES
ALONE.**  `luna_absentcpu_probe.py`'s witness is *"a guest store of 0xfc000000 to INT_ST_MASK1
followed by a store to SOFT_INT1"* -- **unmask, then trigger, both ordinary guest stores, no host
timer and no disk.**  That is exactly the shape a witness for this row needs, and it is why the
`#503` round is worth reading.

**The ISA analogue is not identical**, because there is no soft-interrupt register on this bus: the
PIC mask is already open at reset (so the unmask step is free) but the TRIGGER has to come from a
device asserting, which is what the reachability census now out to codex is enumerating.

*This is the warrant-transfer caution in miniature: a precedent that is genuinely same-family for
one purpose (witness construction) can be wrong for another (disposition), and the row title looks
identical either way.  Read the diff, not the title.*

**THE MINIMAL IMPLEMENTATION, concretely:** add `struct interrupt irq;` and `int
irq_delivery_warned;` to `lca_data` (the existing `memset` initialises the latch);
`INTERRUPT_CONNECT(devinit->interrupt_path, d->irq)` before creating downstream devices, since that
path already defaults to the bootstrap CPU; a `lca_interrupt_notice()` helper carrying the `(once)`
marker; then `notice(); INTERRUPT_ASSERT(d->irq);` and the deassert mirror.  **N = 1 per instance
with an explicit suppression marker -- the house idiom, not the counter form.**

*** IT ALSO CORRECTED ITS OWN EARLIER FOUR-ROW COVERAGE TABLE as having "overstated what could
immediately become passing coverage", which is a seat being harder on itself than on me: ***

    callback forwarding      BUILDABLE TODAY as a host-side test; the current callbacks fail it
                             and the small repair passes it
    masking and release      SPLIT.  Level retention/withdrawal passes after the small repair;
                             masked-versus-unmasked ENTRY requires CPU delivery, and no entry in
                             either case proves nothing about masking
    vector acknowledgement   BLOCKED on missing LCA acknowledgement support -- a SEPARATE missing
                             dependency, implementable independently of CPU dispatch
    guest execution          CANNOT pass with forwarding alone

**SO THE ROUND'S DETECTOR IS THE FIRST ROW PLUS HALF THE SECOND**, and the record must say that
rather than implying the table.

*** AND THE DELIVERY ROUND IS BIGGER THAN A CONDITIONAL IN `cpu_dyntrans.c'. ***  codex found two
more declared-but-unused things in this layer: **the tree WRITES `kentry[]` AND NEVER CONSUMES
IT**, and **`PAL_OSF1_rti` has a printable name with no execution implementation** -- so the PAL
dispatcher cannot supply the interrupt entry/return lifecycle at all.  *That is the fifth
declared-but-unused Alpha item found today, after `ALPHA_PTE_ASM`, `ALPHA_KENTRY_MM` and
`ALPHA_FEATURE_BWX`.*  Queued as its own compatibility round with a named measured delta: on the
partial-repair baseline, an eligible asserted input leaves a guest handler counter unchanged, and
the implementation makes the handler execute and return.

**Footbridge supplies no Alpha PAL entry convention**, so that warrant does NOT transfer to the
delivery round -- only to the propagation shape.

*** THE SIBLING CHECK THE ERROR DEMANDED, AND IT CAME BACK CLEAN. ***  Having overwritten one
committed witness, the obvious question is whether I have done it anywhere else, or whether any
other row's `witness' field names something that is no longer there.  Censused across every OPEN
row:

    open rows                                        194
    of which ALREADY CARRY A WITNESS                 119
    whose witness names a MISSING file                 0

**Zero.**  Every path named in a witness field exists on disk, so this was a single incident and
the restore closed it.  *And all EIGHT high-severity open rows already carry a witness* -- which
says something about the queue that is worth writing down: **the top of this queue is not short of
evidence, it is short of DISPOSITIONS.**  That is the shape of work the flagship adjudication is
for, and it is why the packet's questions are disposition questions rather than requests for more
measurement.

*** THE DISPOSITION QUESTION IS SETTLED, 2026-09-08, AND THE ANSWER IS THAT FORWARDING IS A NO-OP ON
THIS ARCHITECTURE.  Led by the codex seat, VERIFIED BY ME IN ONE GREP. ***

The round had been parked on *"forwarding alone leaves Alpha delivery unresolved"* without anyone
establishing what Alpha delivery actually IS.  A codex ANALYSIS job (see `codexcyberflag` -- the
construction-shaped brief is refused, the analysis-shaped one is not) said mid-stream:

> *"Alpha has a CPU interrupt pin and an `irq_asserted` field, but the searches so far show only
> WRITES to that field."*

**Its stream then ended without a final verdict, so this would have been an UNREAD REVIEW had the
`.err` not been opened.  Checked rather than taken:**

    grep -rn irq_asserted src/          ->  57 references, classified

    cpu_alpha.c:218    cpu->cd.alpha.irq_asserted = 1;      WRITE
    cpu_alpha.c:223    cpu->cd.alpha.irq_asserted = 0;      WRITE
    cpu_alpha.h:161    int irq_asserted;                    DECL
    ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
    READS OF cpu->cd.alpha.irq_asserted ANYWHERE IN src/ :   ZERO

`cpu_dyntrans.c` is where a pending interrupt becomes a delivered one, and it tests exactly three
architectures -- `cd.arm.irq_asserted` (`:208`), `cd.m88k.irq_asserted` (`:212`, `:382`) and
`cd.ppc.irq_asserted` (`:243`).  **Alpha is absent from that list.**  `cpu_ppc.c:309` shows the
same field being consumed on the PPC side; there is no Alpha counterpart.

> **SO THE ALPHA CPU MODEL HAS AN INTERRUPT-PENDING FLAG THAT NOTHING CONSUMES.  Wiring the LCA
> stubs to `cpu_interrupt()` would set a field no code reads: a NO-OP, not a delivery.**

*** WHAT THIS SETTLES, and it changes the round from blocked to shippable: ***

* **Member 7 (IMPLEMENT) is NOT a wiring job.**  It requires adding Alpha interrupt dispatch to
  `cpu_dyntrans.c` plus the PALcode entry and IPL check that go with it -- a SUBSYSTEM, and its own
  round.  The earlier note's instinct that *"declining an interrupt leaves the machine incomplete"*
  was right about the machine and wrong about the size of the gap: the machine is already
  incomplete, before this row's stubs are reached.
* **The partial repair is COHERENT, which was the open question.**  Nothing in the model blocks
  waiting for an acknowledgement that cannot come, because nothing is waiting at all -- there is no
  consumer.  Replacing `exit(1)` with a bounded announce leaves the guest with interrupts silently
  dropped, which is EXACTLY what it already gets on every Alpha path that does not terminate.
* **The honest disclosure the round owes** is therefore not *"we chose not to forward"* but
  *"Alpha interrupt delivery does not exist in this CPU model; these stubs cannot forward to
  anything, and the fix removes a host termination without pretending to add delivery."*

**AND IT REFRAMES THE SEVERITY HONESTLY IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.**  The termination is still
guest-reachable and still witnessed twice (8042 command port, 3/4; ns16550 IRQ 4, 2/4), so the row
stays HIGH.  But the fix buys *the host stops dying*, NOT *interrupts start working* -- and a round
block claiming the latter would be a wrong record.

*Provenance worth keeping: this is the reading-seat-buys-the-class pattern exactly.  codex named the
family (`only writes to that field`) and never finished its answer; one grep turned that into a
measured fact that settles a design question two panels had left open.  The cost of NOT opening a
zero-byte job's `.err` would have been another round of design argument.*

*** PASS 1, 2026-09-08.  P4 SURVIVED A SEAT THAT TRIED TO REFUTE IT, AND FOUR OF MY BRIEF'S OTHER
CLAIMS DID NOT. ***

**grok: "RATIFY member 3 (per-instance, two bits), do not forward, do not call this delivery.
P4 holds and is STRONGER than the brief states."**  On Q1 specifically: *"Yes. I tried to refute it
and failed.  Delivery does not exist."*  **deepseek** conditionally accepted and did the correct
packet-fed thing -- refused to ratify P4 as unverifiable from the packet and named the exact search
that settles it, rather than agreeing.

*** THE FOUR CORRECTIONS, three of which change the round. ***

**(1) Q2 WAS MIS-FRAMED AND THE QUESTION CANNOT BE ASKED.**  I asked whether the stubs should write
`irq_asserted` anyway.  grok: *"`interrupt->extra` is `struct lca_data *`, NOT a `struct cpu *`.
There is no `irq_asserted` in this file to write.  Forwarding is `INTERRUPT_CONNECT(cpu->path, ...)`
plus `INTERRUPT_ASSERT`, i.e. CHIPSET WIRING, not a field store."*  So the option I was weighing does
not exist at these call sites at all -- **the answer is not "no, don't", it is "there is nothing
there to write."**

**(2) "A DRIVER WILL USUALLY REACH BOTH WITHIN ONE INTERRUPT CYCLE" IS FALSE OF THIS CODE, and I
used it to argue for two latch bits.**  grok traced it: *"`isa_interrupt_common` takes ONE EDGE per
call -- ASSERT if IRR went 0->nonzero, DEASSERT if it went nonzero->0, return if the aggregate
stayed asserted.  The 8042 probe never reads the `0x55` reply, so it never deasserts.  The UART probe
leaves IER on and free-runs, so tick keeps asserting.  **Existing witnesses do not touch
`_deassert`.**"*
> **THE CONSEQUENCE IS COVERAGE DEBT AND IT IS DISCLOSED: the deassert latch is UNWITNESSED.**  Two
> bits remain the right choice -- for the opposite reason to the one I gave -- because the two
> callbacks are reached on DIFFERENT edges and a shared bit would report whichever arrived first.

**(3) `detector:` AS THE WITNESS TERM IS A CATEGORY ERROR.**  I proposed it in Q5.  grok: *"That term
is for a fix with a measured detector and NO guest-path witness.  This row already has TWO rung-3
probes.  Unobservable DELIVERY is a CONTRACT fact, not a missing witness of the kill."*  Correct --
the round witnesses the TERMINATION, which is what it fixes; it does not claim to witness delivery,
which it does not add.  The witness term stays `probe:`.

**(4) MY §C0 COUNT WAS STALE** -- see `pass1_20260908/CORRECTION_C0.md`, written before this.  grok's
framing adds the general rule: *"Do not treat a DIRTY-TREE `grep -c` as the ship check."*

*** (5) THE ONE THAT WOULD HAVE SHIPPED A BROKEN ROUND, AND IT NEEDS MEASUREMENT NOT READING. ***

grok: *"The UART probe's `stub named` row is HOSTILE to member 3.  It wants `lca_interrupt_assert`
ABSENT.  A latched `fatal("...TODO")` keeps that row RED FOREVER.  Drop or re-pin it under the
oracle-correction rule; do not ship member 3 against that want."*

**The row is exactly as described:**
`row("stub named", "no" if "lca_interrupt_assert" not in t3 else "yes", "no", ...)`

**BUT THE HAZARD MAY NOT REACH MY IMPLEMENTATION, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE MESSAGE TEXT.**  grok
reasoned from a generic *latched `fatal("...TODO")`* -- keeping the original wording, which contains
the function name.  The announce I wrote says *"[ lca: ISA interrupt assert not implemented (Alpha
has no interrupt delivery); ignored  (once) ]"* -- **"ISA interrupt assert", not
`lca_interrupt_assert`** -- so the forbidden literal may never appear.

> *** THAT IS A READING OF MY OWN STRING AND IT IS EXACTLY THE KIND OF CLAIM THIS PROJECT REQUIRES
> TO BE MEASURED.  The post-fix run settles it; nothing is claimed here. ***  And whichever way it
> lands, grok has identified a REAL DESIGN CONSTRAINT that was not in my brief and that I satisfied
> by accident rather than by intent: **the announce must not contain the literal
> `lca_interrupt_assert`, or it pins a shipped witness row red forever.**

*** THE FIX IS IMPLEMENTED AND MEASURED, 2026-09-08.  ONE INSTRUMENT, BOTH DIRECTIONS. ***

                                     PRE-FIX   POST-FIX
    lca_irqstub_probe.py               3/6       6/6
    lca_irqstub_uart_probe.py          2/5       5/5

Scratch clone `/tmp/gxlca`, baseline `git show HEAD:src/devices/dev_lca.c` rebuilt in the clone.
No project tree mutated.  Raws + a README naming which instrument produced which figure:
`regress/artifacts/lcairqstubkill/fix_20260908/`.

**THE DIFF:** both stubs keep a diagnostic and lose the termination -- option-set member 3, DECLINE
plus a bounded announce.  **PER-INSTANCE** via `interrupt->extra`, not function-static, so one guest
access to one device instance cannot silence every other instance ([[staticlatchscope]]).  **TWO
separate latch bits**, because grok established the two callbacks are reached on DIFFERENT EDGES --
`isa_interrupt_common` takes one edge per call -- so a shared bit would report whichever arrived
first and hide the other entirely.

**THREE ROWS ADDED, because both probes' own contracts demanded them.**  `lca_irqstub_probe.py`'s
header says: *"it is NOT a detector of a repair: 'host survives' would green for a silent return, for
a latched announce, and for an actual interrupt implementation alike.  A fix round owes a row that
discriminates those."*

    irq announce   the announce text is present -- a silent return prints nothing, and a REAL
                   implementation would print nothing either, so only this repair prints this
    irq honest     the announce contains "Alpha has no" -- the round's claim is that it stops the
                   host dying WITHOUT making interrupts work, and this is the only place a reader
                   ever learns that
    irq latched    COUNTS the announce in the free-running UART session, want exactly 1.  That
                   session's tick re-asserts repeatedly, so an unlatched announce prints many times.
                   Counting is the oracle because a PRESENCE row would be satisfied by a latch that
                   never engages -- the very mutant it exists to catch.

*** A DEFECT I INTRODUCED WHILE ADDING THEM, AND CAUGHT BY THE PROBE'S OWN OUTPUT. ***  The rows went
in BELOW each score computation, splitting both scorers: numerator over the old row set, denominator
evaluated at print time.  **The 8042 probe printed SIX ROWS ALL `ok` UNDER A SUMMARY OF 4/6.**  The
UART probe reported 3/5 pre-fix where the honest score was 2/5 -- and post-fix it rendered 5/5
CORRECTLY BY COINCIDENCE, because nothing failed.  Repaired in both files by moving the computation
adjacent to the print.  A census over HEAD shows **0 of 73** candidate probes were ever split, so
both instances were mine; filed as [[splitscorer]] (low) with that correction.

**KNOWN GAP, DISCLOSED IN THE PROBE UNDER CLAUSE (e): `lca_interrupt_deassert` IS WHOLLY
UNWITNESSED.**  Neither witness reaches the deassert edge -- the 8042 probe never reads the `0x55`
reply, and the UART probe leaves IER on and free-runs, so the aggregate never falls back to zero.
Its latch bit and its whole body are uncovered and no mutant of them could be killed.  Closing it
needs a guest sequence that LOWERS the interrupt, which is a new session rather than a new row.  Put
to pass 2 as an explicit question rather than shipped silently.

*** PASS 2: grok returned NOT RATIFY, AND A MUTANT CONFIRMED IT.  My best row was vacuous. ***

**Its verdict:** *"The disposition in `dev_lca.c` is the right one.  The 11-row instrument does not
defend it.  Two floor holes, both from ONE false premise: that UART ticks re-enter
`lca_interrupt_assert`."*

**IT READ THE PATH INSTEAD OF THE BRIEF:** *"`isa_interrupt_common` is EDGE-TRIGGERED on the PIC
aggregate.  If the UART never drops IRR, `irq latched` is vacuous."*

*** MEASURED, NOT CONCEDED.  Mutant `M1_unlatch` removes the latch so the announce fires on EVERY
entry: ***

    base           kbc=6/6   uart=5/5   announce_count=1
    M1_unlatch     kbc=6/6   uart=5/5   announce_count=1     *** CLEAN SWEEP ***

**The count is 1 with and without the latch, because the stub is entered exactly ONCE however long
the guest free-runs.**  My `irq latched` row could not vary under the only mutant it existed to
catch.

> **THIS IS THE CHANNEL FAILURE FOR THE FOURTH TIME IN TWO ROUNDS, AND THE SAME MISTAKE EVERY TIME:
> I named an observable by asking what the code prints on the path I HAD IN MIND, never by tracing
> what the MUTANT actually reaches.**  Here I assumed re-entry; the caller is edge-triggered.

**DISPOSITION -- RELABELLED, NOT DELETED, and the distinction is the honest part.**  The row is
vacuous *as a latch test* and is NOT vacuous *as a statement about behaviour*: the announce really is
emitted once, and pinning that catches a future edit moving it outside the guard.  It is now
`irq once`, its note says it does NOT test the latch, and the measurement is quoted beside it.

*** AND THE CONSEQUENCE IS A GAP THIS ROUND CANNOT CLOSE: THE LATCH IS UNEXERCISED BY ANY WITNESS
IN THIS TREE. ***  Exercising it needs TWO assert edges in one session -- an IRR that falls and rises
again -- which is the SAME missing capability as the unwitnessed deassert path.  So the round ships
a latch it cannot test, and says so under clause (e) rather than implying coverage.

*** A SECOND CORRECTION FROM grok, and it was about to ship in PRODUCT CODE. ***  My comment said
`cpu_dyntrans.c` delivers *"for ARM, M88K and PPC only"*.  Checked: it delivers for **FIVE** --
ARM (`:208`), M88K (`:212`), MIPS via the COP0 exception model (`:219`), PPC (`:243`) and SH via
`int_to_assert` (`:247`).  **I had enumerated by grepping `irq_asserted`, which is a CORRELATE of
delivering rather than the property**, and missed the two that deliver by another mechanism.  *The
fourth correlate-not-the-property error of the day.*  **The Alpha conclusion is unchanged and
STRENGTHENED -- it is the outlier among five, not three** -- and the comment now says so with the
reason, because a wrong reason gets reused.

**grok also CONFIRMED what it could:** P4 holds (two writes of `cd.alpha.irq_asserted`, no reads, no
`DYNTRANS_ALPHA` arm); `interrupt->extra` is a `struct lca_data *` so forwarding is chipset wiring;
and my Q1 reasoning -- the predicates that gated death are the EMPTY SET, because the stubs had no
`if` at all -- is right.

**AND IT WAS EXPLICIT ABOUT WHAT IT DID NOT DO:** *"The scores 6/6 and 5/5 -- I did not re-run the
probes.  I read the artifacts.  Those logs match the brief.  They do NOT show an unlatch mutant."*
That last sentence is the whole finding, stated as a gap in the evidence rather than as an
accusation, and it was correct.

**FIX SHIPPED 2026-09-09 as `#516` (74daefd)**: both stubs de-fatalised, 12-row detector, tables G+H (16 cells, 14 killed, 2 measured equivalent), chain closed on pass 3.  State `in work` until the regress phase runs on it.
rows.hold_question: `lcairqstubkill` IS NOW UNBLOCKED AND I WANT THE DISPOSITION RATIFIED OR REFUSED BEFORE IT SHIPS.  MEASURED: `cpu->cd.alpha.irq_asserted` is WRITTEN at cpu_alpha.c:218/223 and READ NOWHERE -- `cpu_dyntrans.c` dispatches interrupts for arm (:208), m88k (:212, :382) and ppc (:243), and Alpha is absent.  So the Alpha CPU model has an interrupt-pending flag with NO CONSUMER, and wiring the LCA stubs to `cpu_interrupt()` would set a field nothing reads.  THREE QUESTIONS.  (1) Given forwarding is a measured NO-OP, is the right disposition a bounded (once) announce plus a plain return -- member 3 -- with an explicit disclosure that Alpha delivery does not exist?  Or should the round ALSO write `irq_asserted` even though nothing reads it, on the ground that a future Alpha dispatch would then find the state already correct?  I lean AGAINST that: it is the ADDITION LICENCE's 'cannot hurt' shape, and it would ship a line whose only justification is a subsystem nobody has scheduled.  (2) Does removing a host termination without adding delivery need its own SEVERITY restatement in the round block?  The fix buys 'the host stops dying', NOT 'interrupts start working', and I want to be sure the record cannot be read as the latter.  (3) THE WITNESS QUESTION: this row has TWO rung-3 witnesses on independent paths (8042 command port 3/4; ns16550 IRQ 4 2/4).  Both prove the termination.  NEITHER can prove the post-fix behaviour is correct, because 'the host survived and nothing happened' is indistinguishable from 'the host survived and an interrupt was delivered' WHEN NO DELIVERY MECHANISM EXISTS.  Is a detector even constructible here beyond survival plus the latch's own announce, or is this a case where `detector:` is the honest witness term and the contract must say the delivery half is unobservable by construction?

rows.title: dev_uninorth.c: `idata & (1 << dev)` at dev==31 is a signed-shift UB, but NOT guest-visible -- the address port is registered with length 4, so idata can never carry bits 32..63 (investigated and DOWNGRADED, not assumed)
rows.witness: none -- READ, not run.  The arithmetic and the device registration are established; whether an 8-byte guest access can reach the handler (which is what makes bits 32..63 possible) is NOT established and is the row's open question.

entries.grader: main-loop
entries.note: WIDTH/REACHABILITY ANALYSIS.  VERDICT: "NO.  The macppc guest-store paths cannot place bits 32..63 in this register's idata or cur_addr: the dispatcher clamps the four-byte address window before calling the handler.  MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN preserves these access widths."  Verified independently -- see the state_note.

rows.state_note:
FILED 2026-09-07, split out of [[shiftubcensus]] item (A) because it is the only member of that
census with a **GUEST-VISIBLE CONSEQUENCE** rather than a language-level one, and it therefore owes a
witness the others do not.

**THE SITE**, `dev_uninorth.c`, in the PCI address-register write path:

    :56    uint64_t idata = memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len | MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN);
    ...
    :60    d->cur_addr = idata;
    :70    for (dev=11; dev<32; dev++)
    :71        if (idata & (1 << dev))
    :72            break;

**`idata` is `uint64_t` and `1 << dev` is an `int`.**  At `dev == 31` that is `0x80000000`, which as
a signed `int` is NEGATIVE, so converting it for the `&` against a `uint64_t` **SIGN-EXTENDS it to
`0xffffffff80000000`**.

> **CONSEQUENCE IF `idata` CARRIES ANY BIT IN 32..63: the loop matches at `dev == 31` when no
> device bit is set there, and the scan selects the WRONG DEVICE.**  The repair (`1U << dev`) is
> therefore NOT behaviour-preserving here -- unlike its sibling in `dev_v3.c`, where the operand's
> high bits are provably zero and the same edit changes nothing.

**REACHABLE AS A DEVICE:** `machine_macppc.c:68` calls
`dev_uninorth_init(machine, machine->memory, 0xe2000000, ...)`, and `dev_uninorth.c:141` registers
`"uninorth_pci_addr"` at `addr + 0x800000` = **0xe2800000**.  macppc is a supported machine here.

*** WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, AND IT IS THE WHOLE QUESTION: CAN `idata` ACTUALLY CARRY BITS 32..63? ***
`memory_readmax64(cpu, data, len | MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN)` returns a value whose width follows the
ACCESS WIDTH.  On a 4-byte store -- the ordinary way a guest writes a PCI config address -- the
result cannot exceed 32 bits, the sign-extended ones meet only zeros, and **nothing observable
happens**.  The defect needs an **8-byte** access to that register.

**So the row is HELD at the reachability question, not at the arithmetic.**  A codex analysis is out
on exactly this (`regress/artifacts/shiftubcensus/UNINORTH_brief.md`), asking: what does
`memory_readmax64` return per width; what widths reach this handler on macppc; and -- the premise I
am least sure of -- whether `MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, which is OR'd into the `len` PARAMETER, can
perturb the length itself rather than only the byte order.

**SEVERITY DELIBERATELY LEFT AT `med` PENDING THAT ANSWER.**  If an 8-byte access reaches the
handler this is a guest-drivable mis-decode on a supported machine and should be HIGH; if it cannot,
this collapses into the same language-level hygiene as the other two census members and should be
LOW.  *Grading it before the answer would be picking the number I prefer.*

**THE REPAIR IS ONE TOKEN EITHER WAY** (`1U << dev`), and it is correct under both outcomes -- the
question is only what the round may CLAIM, and whether it owes a witness.

*** MY SHAKIEST PREMISE IS ANSWERED BY READING, AND IT ANSWERS THE REASSURING WAY -- SO THE ROW
NARROWS TO EXACTLY ONE QUESTION. ***

I flagged as least certain whether `MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN`, OR'd into the **`len` parameter**, could
perturb the LENGTH rather than only the byte order.  `src/core/memory.c`:

    #define MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN   128           (memory.h:98)

    uint64_t memory_readmax64(struct cpu *cpu, unsigned char *buf, int len)
    {
            int i, byte_order = cpu->byte_order;
            uint64_t x = 0;

            if (len & MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN) {
                    len &= ~MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN;      <- EXPLICITLY STRIPPED
                    byte_order = EMUL_LITTLE_ENDIAN;
            }
            ... for (i=0; i<len; i++) { x <<= 8; x |= buf[i]; }

**The flag is stripped from `len` before it is used as a count, so it cannot change the length.**
And the two cannot collide in practice: the flag is 128 while access widths are 1..8.

**WHAT THAT LEAVES, and it is now the WHOLE question:** `x` accumulates exactly `len` bytes, so

    len == 4  ->  x <= 0xffffffff, bits 32..63 are ZERO  ->  the sign-extended ones meet only
                  zeros and NOTHING OBSERVABLE HAPPENS
    len == 8  ->  x can carry bits 32..63                ->  the spurious dev==31 match is REAL

> **So the row turns entirely on: can a guest issue an 8-BYTE access to `0xe2800000` on macppc, and
> does it reach this handler with `len == 8` intact?**  Nothing else matters -- not the endianness
> flag, not the arithmetic, both of which are now settled.

*Recorded because narrowing a question is worth as much as answering one, and because this half was
settled by reading two functions while a seat works the other half.  The codex analysis in flight is
asked the same thing independently; if it disagrees about the stripping, the disagreement is
checkable in four lines.*

*** ANSWERED: **NO**.  THE ROW IS DOWNGRADED med -> low, AND THE INVESTIGATION IS WHY THE SEVERITY
WAS LEFT UNGRADED IN THE FIRST PLACE. ***

codex: *"The macppc guest-store paths cannot place bits 32..63 in this register's `idata` or
`cur_addr`: the dispatcher clamps the four-byte address window before calling the handler.
`MEM_PCI_LITTLE_ENDIAN` preserves these access widths."*  **Both halves verified here rather than
accepted:**

    dev_uninorth.c:141-142   memory_device_register(mem, "uninorth_pci_addr", addr + 0x800000,
                                 4, dev_uninorth_addr_access, d, DM_DEFAULT, NULL);
                                 ^-- REGISTERED LENGTH 4

    memory_rw.c:495          if (paddr + len > mem->devices[i].length)   <- truncates, with the
                                 fork's own #91/#93/#94 per-device note above it

So an 8-byte guest store to `0xe2800000` is **truncated to 4 bytes before the handler runs**.
`memory_readmax64` then accumulates at most 4 bytes, `idata <= 0xffffffff`, bits 32..63 are ZERO,
and the sign-extended ones in `0xffffffff80000000` meet only zeros.  **Nothing observable happens.**

> **SO THIS COLLAPSES INTO THE SAME LANGUAGE-LEVEL HYGIENE AS THE OTHER TWO [[shiftubcensus]]
> MEMBERS.**  The shift is still UB and still worth the one-token repair; what is retracted is the
> claim that it mis-decodes a device.

*** THE PROCESS POINT IS THE VALUE HERE. ***  The arithmetic was right, the device really is
instantiated on a supported machine, and the sign-extension really would select the wrong device --
**every step held except reachability, and reachability is what decided it.**  Had the row been
graded HIGH on the arithmetic alone it would have carried a guest-visible claim that is false, and a
fix round would have been designed around a witness that cannot exist.  *Leaving the number blank
cost one codex invocation and bought a correct grade.*

**A DETAIL WORTH KEEPING:** the sibling `uninorth_pci_data` port at `+0xc00000` IS registered with
length **8** (`:143-144`).  So the width concern is not absurd in general for this device -- it is
simply wrong for the ADDRESS port, which is the one with the shift.  A future reader tempted to
generalise "uninorth clamps to 4" should not.

rows.title: _guest-src-openbsd22/ holds 8,138 .c files of contemporary guest OS source covering six of this fork's emulation targets, and NOTHING in the carrier or harness mentions it -- I called a chipset question unanswerable one paragraph before a seat answered it from there

rows.state_note:
FILED 2026-09-07.  **NOT a defect -- a RESOURCE this project has and does not know it has**, filed
because I declared a hardware question unanswerable from this machine one paragraph before a seat
answered it from a file on disk.

*** `_guest-src-openbsd22/` SITS AT THE PROJECT ROOT AND CONTAINS THE ACTUAL GUEST OS SOURCE. ***
Derived rather than transcribed:

    8,138  .c files
    architectures: alpha  amiga  arc  arm32  atari  hp300  i386  kbus  m68k  mac68k  mvme68k
                   mvme88k  pc532  pmax  powerpc  sparc  sun3  vax  wgrisc

**Six of those are this fork's own emulation targets** -- `alpha` (alphabook1), `arc`, `arm32`,
`mvme88k` (the m88k/luna family), `pmax` (DECstation) and `powerpc` (macppc).  It is OpenBSD 2.2,
dated 1997, i.e. CONTEMPORARY with the hardware these device models emulate.

**IT IS NOT IN THE REPO.**  It lives at the project root, outside `GXEMUL-SEC/`, untracked -- which
is why nothing in the carrier or the harness mentions it and why a fresh session has no way to learn
it exists.

*** THE MEASURED PAYOFF, on the day it was noticed. ***  Working `lcaconfbus1kill`, I wrote into the
ledger that whether `ioc_conf & 1` is a bus selector or a cycle type is *"a statement about the
21066 ... not CHECKED here"*, because `_scratchpad/` holds no LCA datasheet.  The codex seat then
cited `_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/alpha/pci/lca_pci.c`, and reading it settled the question
outright:

    :103   *bp = (tag >> 16) & 0xff;      /*  bus      */
    :106   *dp = (tag >> 11) & 0x1f;      /*  device   */
    :127   if (secondary) { ... REGVAL(LCA_IOC_CONF) = 0x01; ... }

That is the fix's decode verbatim, plus proof that the register selects the configuration FORMAT.
**And it converted the row's own caution -- "NOT CLAIMED: that any shipped guest issues this
sequence" -- into the opposite finding: the sequence IS the driver's secondary-bus path.**

> **WHY THIS BEATS A DATASHEET FOR THIS PROJECT'S QUESTIONS.**  The recurring question here is not
> *what does the hardware do* but *what does a guest actually do* -- is a path travelled, is a
> register written, does a driver depend on this behaviour.  The witness ladder itself ranks a boot
> above a probe for exactly that reason ("a probe proves a path CAN be reached; a boot proves it IS
> travelled").  **A contemporary driver for the emulated chipset answers that class directly, and it
> is greppable in seconds.**

**PROPOSED, NOT DONE: a carrier line.**  `CLAUDE.md` tells a reader to `ls _scratchpad/*.pdf` before
reasoning from first principles about a device, and records that an absent-source note was
load-bearing and wrong for twelve days.  **This is the same shape one directory over**, and the
analogous line would be: *before calling a guest-behaviour or chipset question unanswerable, grep
`_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/<arch>/`.*  Editing the carrier is an owner-facing act and section J
checks its tracked copy, so it is **filed as a candidate for the 2026-09-09 adjudication** rather
than done unilaterally.

**A CAUTION THAT BELONGS WITH IT:** OpenBSD 2.2 is ONE guest at ONE version.  What it does is
evidence that a real driver does it; what it does NOT do is not evidence that no guest does.  And
the fork's models are not obliged to match this driver -- they are obliged to match the HARDWARE, of
which this is a well-informed second-hand reading.  *Cite it as "the OpenBSD 2.2 driver does X", never
as "the hardware does X".*

*** A SECOND MEASURED PAYOFF, 2026-09-08 -- AND IT IS ALSO A MEASURED COST, WHICH STRENGTHENS THE
CASE FOR THE FILED CARRIER LINE RATHER THAN WEAKENING IT. ***

Working `lcaconfbus1kill` again, I opened `sys/arch/alpha/pci/lca_pci.c` and derived four findings
-- the `REGVAL(LCA_IOC_CONF) = 0x01` secondary-bus write, the `(pcireg_t)-1` initialisation that
normalises absence to all-ones at any offset, the `1 << (device + 11)` IDSEL frob, and the tag
decomposition.  **All four were already in that row's note, several verbatim.**  I had read the
first part of the note and not the guest-source section.

> **SO THE RESOURCE IS NOW ESTABLISHED AS VALUABLE TWICE OVER, AND THE FAILURE MODE HAS CHANGED
> SHAPE: it is no longer "nobody knows the tree exists" but "the findings FROM it are scattered
> across row notes, so they get re-derived."**  The filed carrier line -- *before calling a
> guest-behaviour question unanswerable, grep `_guest-src-openbsd22/sys/arch/<arch>/`* -- addresses
> the first.  **It does not address the second**, and a reader deciding on it should know that: what
> would address the second is a single place where guest-source findings land, which is a different
> and larger proposal that I am NOT making here.

*The carrier line remains FILED, not done.  Two inventory entries were added to the carrier's PDF
list today (the Alpha 21066 and ARM DDI 0406C.d), which is the existing list's own pattern; a new
behavioural RULE is the thing this row deliberately reserved for the owner, and it stays reserved.*

entries.hold_question: `armbfiwidth` IS THE THIRD SITE OF AN IDIOM `#510` FIXED AT TWO, AND SIX SEATS AGREE ITS FORM DOES NOT TRANSFER -- so the question is not whether to fix it but WHAT THE ROUND MAY CLAIM.  SETTLED: UBFX/SBFX encode widthm1 so their width is never negative, while BFI encodes MSB so `width = msb - lsb + 1' reaches [-30, 32]; of 1024 encodable (msb,lsb) pairs, 468 reach an undefined shift and 465 of those also have architecturally invalid ordering.  The prescribed fix is `mask = (width <= 0) ? 0U : ((width == 32) ? 0xffffffffU : ((1U << width) - 1))'.  AND THE ARM MANUAL IS NOW LOCAL AND READ: ddi0406.txt:18066 (A8.8.20) gives `if msbit >= lsbit ... else UNPREDICTABLE', with NO required destination value.  THREE QUESTIONS.  (1) THE ROUND'S CLAIM: codex warns this is NOT definedness-only -- at width 32 the manual says BFI copies the whole register (`<width>' is 1 to 32-<lsb>), while under the count-masked host lowering `#510' describes, the OLD mask would be zero and leave the destination unchanged.  So a guest-visible BEHAVIOUR CORRECTION may be hiding inside what I would otherwise write up as a definedness repair, and NEITHER of us has measured that lowering at BFI.  Does the round owe that measurement before it may ship, or is an explicit disclosure enough?  (2) POLICY versus ARCHITECTURE: for `msbit < lsbit' the manual says UNPREDICTABLE and mandates nothing, so `mask = 0' (preserve the destination) is an EMULATOR POLICY choice.  Is silently preserving right, or does an UNPREDICTABLE encoding deserve a once-only announcement?  The tree has precedent for both and no universal policy.  (3) THE DETECTOR: `#510`'s own finding is that `1 << 31' and `1U << 31' give the SAME mask after the `- 1', so NO guest-value row can kill a `1U' -> `1' regression -- only UBSAN or a source pin can.  Given that, what may this round's detector honestly claim to cover, and does the disclosed `ubsanshiftlane' debt have to land first?

This is the adjudicator hat, not an independent seat review; it is recorded as fable5 because that is the seat the hold names.  RULING on the three questions.
